# Deep structures: a world without a centre {#sec-ch01}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Preliminary draft --- under review.** Published for review; content, figures and citations may still change.

::: {.chapter-subtitle}
Before prices, the only measure of integration is the diffusion of goods and ideas.
:::

> "Ships from Meluhha, ships from Magan, and ships from Dilmun he made tie up alongside the quay of Agade."
> — inscription of Sargon of Akkad, c.2300 BCE

## Follow one thing {.unnumbered}

Follow a bead. Sometime around 2500 BCE an artisan in one of the Indus cities took a piece of hard orange carnelian, drilled it lengthwise with a slow stone drill, and etched a white pattern into its surface by a technique that was, for the moment, a Harappan monopoly. The bead travelled. It went down the Indus, along the coast of the Arabian Sea, up the Persian Gulf through the entrepots of Magan and Dilmun, and ended in a grave at Ur, some two thousand kilometres from the hand that made it, and a good deal further by the route it actually took. No contract survives to tell us who carried it, what was paid, or at what price.

The bead itself is the evidence — that two distant economies had touched, that goods and standards moved between them, and that an exchange existed at all. This is how the whole of this chapter must be read: in a world before coins and price-lists, integration is visible only in things, in the diffusion of goods and shared measures rather than in any record of a market.

And the bead carried one more clue, in the direction it travelled. Indus goods reached Sumer, and Meluhhan ships docked in Sumerian ports, while much less Mesopotamian material has been found in the Indus. In a period with no prices to compare, an asymmetry like that is the crudest available sign of who held the initiative. It is also a treacherous one, and this chapter takes it apart later — beginning with the observation that a carnelian bead is exactly the kind of thing that survives to be counted. But it does place the Indus, in its first appearance in this book, among the most active traders of a world that did not yet have a centre.^[**Sources:** Dalrymple (Loc 1163, 1168) on the Meluhha trade and the goods reaching Ur; Anthony (loc 4821) on carnelian moving west. **Read more:** Dalrymple, *The Golden Road* (2024).]

![The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro --- the planned monumentality of the Indus cities, built without the palaces or royal tombs of contemporary Mesopotamia and Egypt. Photo: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0.](book/figures/photos/div-indus.jpg){#fig-greatbath width=80%}

## Where we are on the arc {.unnumbered}

This is the first chapter, and it is the one place in the book where the central question cannot yet be asked. The book exists to test a claim — that the weight of the world economy sat in Asia for far longer than we tend to assume — period by period, against the evidence. But "where did the weight sit?" only means something once there is a single connected economy whose weight can be located, and across these three thousand years there was not one. There were several loosely linked riverine cores, trading at the edges, rising and falling on their own clocks, but no integrated system with a centre of gravity to find. So this chapter returns no verdict on the spine; it builds the ground the spine will later stand on, laying down the geography — the monsoon and the three great channels — that will eventually make the Indian Ocean the natural integrator.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe (Loc 158) on the channels frame; Pearson (Ch.1) on the monsoon deep structure. **Read more:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015).]

![Centre-of-gravity locator: in c.3500--500 BCE there was no single centre to locate --- only several loosely linked riverine cores, keyed west to east: (a) Egypt, (b) Mesopotamia/Uruk, (c) the Indus (Harappa), and (d) the forming East Asian core. The Near East (Uruk) was the most connected node and the Indus the most active long-distance trader; the spine is not yet applicable, and the chapter's contribution is structural (stylised; not to scale). Author's schematic.](book/figures/cog-locator-01.png){#fig-cog01 width=100%}

## The stage and the cast

The stage was built by geology and weather. A continental collision some fifty million years ago raised the Himalayas, and the mountains organised the climate of half the world: they created the monsoon, the great reversing wind that blows from the south-west in the northern summer and swings back from the north-east in winter, and they fed the river basins — the Indus, the Ganges, and by analogy the Yellow and Yangtze — where the first surplus-producing societies grew up.

The monsoon's deepest gift was reliability. Because the wind reversed on a known schedule, a sailor could ride out on one season's breath and return on the other, which made predictable round-trip voyaging possible across the Indian Ocean in a way the Atlantic and Pacific could not match. That reliability is what the geographer Michael Pearson called the ocean's "deep structure," and it is the master variable of this whole book.

But it set possibilities, not outcomes — a stage, not a script. Three corridors were born in these millennia and would carry goods, people and ideas for the next four thousand years: the maritime Indian Ocean, the desert-and-oasis route later called the Silk Road, and the great Eurasian steppe. Around them sat the cast — the riverine cores that could generate a tradable surplus.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe (Loc 158) on the steppe corridor and the three channels; Pearson (Ch.1) on the monsoon deep structure. **Read more:** Pearson, *The Indian Ocean* (2003).]

![Orientation: the stage and the three channels. The riverine cores --- Mesopotamia/Uruk, the Indus (Harappa), Egypt and the forming East Asian core --- linked at the edges by the maritime Indian Ocean (still waiting), the desert/oasis route, and the Eurasian steppe (the era's dynamic engine), with the Gulf trade running Indus $\to$ Dilmun $\to$ Sumer (stylised; not to scale). Author's schematic.](book/figures/map-channels-01.png){#fig-channels width=100%}

## Dramatis personae
The economic actors of c.3500--500 BCE, profiled east to west. There is no centre yet, so these are loosely linked cores rather than partners in one system. **India appears in every chapter at the fullest depth** --- here as the Indus civilisation, the period's most active long-distance trader on the evidence that survives — a qualification the chapter goes on to make good. The steppe comes last not as a periphery but as the era's dynamic engine.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The forming East Asian core

The Yellow and Yangtze valleys were taking shape as an agrarian world in their own right while the Gulf trade ran in the west, but they sat largely outside it. Wild rice was being gathered along the Yangtze from about 8000 BCE, cultivated from about 6000, and fully domesticated in the lower Yangtze only around 4000 to 3000 BCE, and by 3000 BCE farming had spread across much of what would become the East Asian core; the first Chinese state emerged around 1800 BCE. This was a populous, river-fed agrarian base of the same broad type as Mesopotamia or the Indus, generating surplus and supporting dense settlement, but it grew up on its own metabolism rather than as a node in the western relay.^[**Sources:** Fuller, Qin et al., "The domestication process and domestication rate in rice", *Science* 323 (2009), and Kingwell-Banham, Petrie and Fuller in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 2, for the staged chronology; Anthony (loc 7344). **Note on a date corrected:** an earlier draft gave 9,500-7,500 BCE, following Mithen (2003); that is the Diaotonghuan-era dating and has been superseded. **Read more:** Fuller, Qin et al. (2009).]

What marks the core out for this period is how late the western bronze-and-chariot package reached it. The earliest known chariots come from Sintashta graves in the Urals, before 2000 BCE; the type was in the Near East by the nineteenth century BCE, yet it did not appear in China until about 1200 BCE — arriving by way of the steppe, not the Gulf. The same was broadly true of the metallurgy that defined the Bronze Age elsewhere. So the East Asian core was forming on a parallel track, connected to the wider system, if at all, only through the long grass corridor to its north and west.^[**Sources:** Anthony (loc 6171); Cunliffe (loc 1266, 2001). **Read more:** Anthony, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* (2007).]

Two states then carried the core through the rest of this chapter's span, and the first of them left records.

The Shang (c.1600--1046 BCE) were northern China's first securely documented state, and they cast bronze at something close to industrial scale: foundries at Zhengzhou and Anyang, ritual vessels surviving in the thousands, the largest of them weighing over 800 kilograms. Their expansion followed commodities, north-east toward the Bohai salt and south toward metal, with jade, ivory, cowries and turquoise moving on top of that. They also left the oracle bones, the earliest Chinese writing, and the contrast with Mesopotamia is sharp enough to be worth pausing on: cuneiform began as accounting, while the oracle bones are records of divination. The two earliest writing systems in this book were made to preserve different things, which shapes what each civilisation can now be asked about. One thing the Shang did not invent was the chariot, in royal use by about 1200 BCE and unmistakably a debt to the steppe. The core was independent, but it was not sealed.^[**Sources:** Liu & Chen (2012) on Shang bronze casting at Zhengzhou and Anyang; Anthony (loc 6171) on the chariot reaching China c.1200 BCE. The very large surviving vessel (the Houmuwu ding, over 800 kg) is Shang and from Anyang; the often-quoted figure of some twelve thousand inscribed vessels is Zhou-era, and the two should not be merged. **Read more:** Liu & Chen, *The Archaeology of China* (2012).]

The Zhou who followed show state capacity arriving well before anything an economist would call a market.

Western Zhou (1045--771 BCE) was a patrimonial arrangement in von Glahn's reading: the king shared authority with noble houses and lived off rights over land and labour, a domain state rather than a tax state, its three ministries named for Lands, Construction and Horses. Exchange ran between aristocratic lineages, and markets in any ordinary sense were absent; this was a world of obligation rather than of wages. Eastern Zhou (770--256 BCE), and the Warring States contest that ran on to Qin's unification in 221, then ground capacity out of endemic war --- conscription, censuses, uniform weights, deliberate grain-price smoothing by about 400 BCE, primogeniture abolished in the 350s --- while iron lifted farm output and coinage pulled interregional trade and specialisation, iron in Hann, salt in Qi, gold in Chu. The sequence is the counter-intuitive part. The instinct is to assume markets came first and states arrived later to regulate them; here the state came first, by a wide margin.^[**Sources:** von Glahn (2016) on the Western Zhou as a patrimonial domain state and on Warring-States fiscal and administrative capacity; Scott (Page 631) on early state formation. **Read more:** von Glahn, *The Economic History of China* (2016).]

A warning has to travel with all of this, and it is sharper than a general complaint about thin evidence. The bias is in the writing medium. Mesopotamia kept its accounts on clay, which survives when a city burns; early China kept its on bamboo and wood slips, which do not begin to survive in the archaeological record until about the fifth century BCE. What we have from Shang China is therefore inscriptions meant for display, above all the oracle bones, and Wang Haicheng's point is that the vast majority of bones cracked for divination were never inscribed at all, while everyday administrative documents were almost certainly written on perishable materials and are simply gone. The graph for a bundle of writing slips appears in the divination texts themselves, so the Shang were keeping records on slips; we just cannot read them.

So a comparison between a bureaucratic, account-keeping Mesopotamia and a ritual, divining China may be substantially a comparison between clay and bamboo. That does not make the western record false, but it does mean the eastern core is under-documented for this era rather than demonstrably marginal, and that absence of data is not absence of activity.^[**Sources:** Wang Haicheng, "Writing and the city in early China", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 3 (2015), pp. 131-57, on perishable media, the survival threshold of about the fifth century BCE, display writing, and the uninscribed divination bones; Mithen (Loc 7937) and Scott (Page 100) on the general preservation asymmetry. **Read more:** Wang (2015).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** — little evidence of long-distance export into the western system this early; the core's surplus was consumed and circulated locally.
- **Main imports** — the bronze-and-chariot technology package, arriving overland from the steppe around 1200 BCE rather than by sea.
- **Export markets** — none securely attested in the Gulf or Mesopotamian record for this period.
- **Import sources** — the Eurasian steppe corridor to the north and west, the one channel that reached it.^[**Sources:** Anthony (loc 6171); Mithen (Loc 7945). **Read more:** Mithen, *After the Ice* (2003).]
:::

## The Indus civilisation — the agency-holder

The Indus, or Harappan, civilisation grew up along the Indus and its tributaries from roughly 3000 BCE, when its first cities appeared at much the same moment as the Early Dynastic cities of Sumer, and it reached its mature urban phase between about 2600 and 1900 BCE. Its base was agrarian, like every economy in this chapter. What set the Harappans apart was how much of what they built on it had been *designed*: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out to a plan, with gridded streets, fired-brick housing and elaborate covered drains, at a degree of urban engineering with no contemporary equal. Mohenjo-daro covered more than 200 hectares, within reach of Uruk's 250, and Harappan urban sites ran from about 50 hectares to over 200. The distinguishing feature was not size but deliberation.

The settlement pattern is the stranger fact. Mature Harappan material turns up at more than a thousand sites spread over more than a million square kilometres, and of those only five count as urban: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira. The rest are typically around five hectares.

Those five stand far apart, 280 kilometres from Mohenjo-daro to Ganweriwala and 600 from Harappa to Mohenjo-daro, across a territory the size of western Europe. Mesopotamia in the same centuries was a crowded landscape of neighbouring cities within a few days' walk of one another. The Indus was a handful of very large places in a very large space, and whatever held it together was not proximity.

Two of the things this economy stood on were domesticated locally, which matters for a region routinely written up as a recipient of other people's innovations: zebu cattle at or around Mehrgarh, and the earliest evidence anywhere for Indian tree cotton, on which a textile tradition rests that later chapters follow for four thousand years.

Mehrgarh's own dating has just moved, and sharply: the excavation's surviving team, radiocarbon-dating tooth enamel rather than the root-contaminated charcoal the old chronology rested on, now put its aceramic Neolithic at 5250 to 4650 BCE rather than beginning around 7000 or 8000. The cotton, from a grave in that phase, moves with it. Nothing about the local-domestication argument depends on the older dates, but a great deal of popular writing about Mehrgarh does.^[**Sources:** Roy (p.20) on the Indus settlements beginning c.3000 BCE, contemporary with Early Dynastic Sumer; Mohan (Loc 531) on the end of the urban era c.1900 BCE; Kingwell-Banham, Petrie and Fuller, "Early agriculture in South Asia", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 2 (2015), pp. 261–309, on zebu domestication at Mehrgarh and on the tree-cotton evidence, which rests on Moulherat et al., "First evidence of cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh", *Journal of Archaeological Science* 29 (2002), which itself places the grave in the first half of the sixth millennium BCE; on the redating, Mutin et al., "New radiocarbon dates of human tooth enamel reveal a late appearance of farming life in the Indus Valley", *Scientific Reports* 15 (2025), 11345, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-92621-5, whose co-authors include one of the original excavators; Sinopoli, "Ancient South Asian cities in their regions", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 3 (2015), pp. 319–42, at pp. 322, 324–25 and 330, for the urban site count, the 50-to-200-plus hectare range, Mohenjo-daro's extent, the intercity distances and the five-hectare norm for non-urban sites. Older syntheses give appreciably smaller figures for the great cities — Chakrabarti (1979), pp. 210–11, via Allchin (1995), p. 202, puts Harappa and Mohenjo-daro at about 85 hectares each — but Sinopoli's are the current figures and are used here. **Read more:** Kingwell-Banham, Petrie and Fuller (2015).]

Two features of the internal economy stand out, and the second is genuinely puzzling. The first was standardisation, and it went further than the phrase usually implies. Harappan cubical stone weights double in a binary sequence up to a standard of about 13.7 grams and then continue in decimal multiples, the largest at Mohenjo-daro reaching almost eleven kilograms — a system, not a convention, and one exported as far as the Gulf. Fired bricks hold a 1:2:4 ratio across the whole settled zone. That last uniformity is where the state instinct should be resisted: Kenoyer's explanation is not a building code but a class of brickmakers whose craft tradition spread from settlement to settlement. Alongside the weights ran a corpus of inscribed seals, and the two together are the apparatus of an economy in which goods were measured, marked and exchanged to common conventions over long distances.

The second feature is what the cities lack, and the usual shorthand overstates it. There are no royal tombs, no monumental religious architecture, no royal iconography and no depictions of warfare. Two entries on that list need care: temples are not securely absent, since Kenoyer allows that House AI at Mohenjo-daro may have been one; and no depictions of warfare is not the same as no warfare, because skeletal remains from Harappa carry clear evidence of interpersonal violence. What is absent is a palace *quarter* — the largest buildings are scattered across the mounds rather than gathered into a royal precinct — and the structures long called granaries have gone too, having produced no charred grain, no storage vessels and no sealings. What these cities were reticent about was the display of personal power, which is not the same as being socially flat: Possehl, who denies this was a state, still writes of upper ranks and a social pyramid, and remarks that the Great Bath was not the playground of the Indus *hoi polloi*.^[**Sources:** Kenoyer, *Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization* (1998), on the weight sequence, the brick ratio and the brickmakers' craft tradition; Possehl, *The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective* (2002), on Mohenjo-daro's largest buildings, the social pyramid and the Great Bath, and on the rejection of the granaries. Both are cited by chapter where the held edition lacks pagination. **Read more:** Kenoyer (1998).]

How such a civilisation was governed, and how its surplus was gathered without the visible apparatus of monarchy, is the liveliest question in Indus archaeology, and it is worth giving students the argument rather than a verdict. Three positions are in play.

They run as a spectrum rather than a quarrel. Kenoyer argues for rulers of a kind, reading the weight system as established by them, plausibly for taxation. Possehl denies a state in the archaic sense — no king, no royal apparatus — but affirms elites, ranks and authority perhaps sitting in councils. Adam Green goes further, arguing for collective governance in which many intersecting institutions rather than any ruling class coordinated labour and produced the public goods. @sec-appE sets the three out, and the evidence that divides them: it turns largely on where the seals were found, and the same distribution supports Green's reading and Possehl's depending how it is weighed.

One fact cuts across all three readings: no Indus seal has ever been found in a burial, which is exactly where Egypt and Mesopotamia put the marks of individual status.

What the three agree on is enough to carry the economic argument without settling the dispute. There were no kings, no royal display and no depictions of warfare; there was extensive investment in urban public goods — house-by-house wells, bathing platforms, covered drains — and there was a standardisation apparatus reaching from villages to the Gulf. A society can build all of that without anyone's name on it.

This matters beyond the Indus. The chapters that follow spend a great deal of time on states that taxed, borrowed, minted and spent, and it is easy to slide from that into assuming an economy needs a visible sovereign before it can build anything. The Harappans built more urban infrastructure per head than any of their contemporaries and left no king's name attached to any of it. Who commanded that effort is genuinely unresolved.^[**Sources:** Kenoyer, *Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization* (1998), for rulers and the weight system; Possehl, *The Indus Civilization* (2002), for the no-state-but-elites position and the reading of seal findspots; Green, "Of Revenue Without Rulers: Public Goods in the Egalitarian Cities of the Indus Civilization", *Frontiers in Political Science* 4 (2022), open access, for collective governance, the Mohenjo-daro seal count after Mackay and the household distribution after Franke-Vogt, and the Harappa gateway weights after Kenoyer and Miller (2007); Kenoyer (1998) on the absence of seals from burials. Green's comparative framework is Blanton and Fargher's, in which societies drawing on internal revenue such as agrarian taxation tend to produce more public goods and wider political participation than those living off external resources. **Read more:** Green (2022), open access.]

With no prices and no ledgers, the integration the Harappans achieved cannot be read off a market. It is read from the things themselves: Harappan seals, cubical weights and above all etched carnelian beads turn up in Mesopotamian contexts, and carnelian from the Indus borderlands was moving north through the Caucasus by the late fourth millennium. Indus craft and Indus measures in distant markets, not any record of transactions, are the evidence that a long-distance economy existed at all.^[**Sources:** Anthony (loc 4821, 4896) on carnelian from western Pakistan moving north via the Maikop conduit c.3700--3400 BCE; Dalrymple (Loc 1163, 1168) on teak, ivory and the Meluhha trade reaching Mesopotamia. **Read more:** Dalrymple, *The Golden Road* (2024).]

Externally, the Harappans ran the period's great long-distance trade, the Gulf route that linked the Indus — the Meluhha of the cuneiform records — to Mesopotamia through the intermediary ports of Magan, on the Oman coast, and Dilmun, the entrepot on Bahrain.

What moved is set out in the trade profile below; two qualifications matter more than the inventory. The first is that few ships sailed the whole way. The traffic moved in stages, and in the Ur III period Mesopotamian boats went only as far as Magan, and later only to Dilmun, even though most of what they collected there had started in India. Dilmun grew rich precisely because the route was broken in the middle. The second is that the westward flow was not the whole story. Meluhhan boats put in at Sargon's quay at Akkad, and an Akkadian seal inscription names an interpreter of Meluhha — there were Harappans in Mesopotamia, and enough of them to need translating. But Mesopotamian weights have turned up at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, and in one Harappan cemetery a young woman was buried wrapped in a reed shroud inside a wooden coffin, a rite unknown in the Indus world and familiar from Ur and Kish. Somebody from Mesopotamia lived, and died, in India.^[**Sources:** Ratnagar, *Encounters: The Westerly Trade of the Harappa Civilization* (1981), on transshipment and the staged character of the route, the dragoman inscription (after Gelb 1968), the Mesopotamian weights, and the Cemetery R 37 burial (after Wheeler 1947); Dalrymple (Loc 1163, 1168) on the goods reaching Ur. Note Edzard's caution, reported by Ratnagar, that not every textual mention of Dilmun or Meluhha need refer to the people of those lands. **Read more:** Ratnagar, *Encounters* (1981).]

What survives is not a clean asymmetry but a changing one. Through the mature phase the initiative ran west: Harappan goods, standards and people are far more visible in Mesopotamia than the reverse, and no Mesopotamian commercial text records trade with Meluhha at all, the references being royal and tributary. Later the balance shifted, once Harappan ports on the Makran coast came within reach of sailors who did not have to cross open-ocean monsoon water, and the carrying passed increasingly to Mesopotamians and Dilmunites. Agency followed the sailing conditions and the position of the ports rather than belonging to anyone. Carry that forward carefully: who carried the goods is a fact about shipping capability and who bore the voyage risk, not about who captured the gains, which turns on each side's alternatives — and Mesopotamia had the deeper pockets. The proposition the rest of this book uses is the safer one, that whoever could reach the other party on their own terms was better placed to take the larger share.

One further caution bites hardest of all, and it is about what each side sent. Indus exports were carnelian beads, seals, ivory and stone weights: hard, distinctive, durable objects that survive four thousand years and are identifiable at a glance as Harappan. Mesopotamia sent back silver, tin, wool, oil and grain, which were consumed, remelted, rotted, or survive without being identifiable as Mesopotamian at all. An exchange of exactly equal value in both directions would leave a lopsided record, tilted the way this one is tilted. That does not dissolve the asymmetry — the Harappan presence includes people and standards, not only goods — but it does mean the record cannot carry the weight the strong version of the claim puts on it. It is the same survival logic the chapter uses in the Indus's favour elsewhere, running the other way.^[**Sources:** Ratnagar, *Encounters* (1981), for the absence of Meluhha from Mesopotamian commercial texts, the tributary character of the Akkadian-period references, and the argument that trade handling passed to Mesopotamians and Dilmunites once the Makran ports were in use. **Read more:** Ratnagar, *Encounters* (1981).]^[**Sources:** Dalrymple (Loc 1163, 1168) on the Meluhha trade and the goods reaching Ur and Mesopotamia; Roy (p.27) on the long-run pattern of ships carrying goods to and from India. **Read more:** Dalrymple, *The Golden Road* (2024).]

The urban phase ended around 1900 BCE: the great cities were given up, the weights-and-seals apparatus fell out of use, and the population shifted east toward the Ganges. The decline was broadly coincident with the weakening of the monsoon at the 4.2 ka event, and the temptation to read one as the cause of the other should be resisted — starting with the arithmetic. The 4.2 ka event is around 2200 BCE and the de-urbanisation around 1900: three centuries apart, which is a long time for a cause to take effect. The palaeoclimate record shows no drought of the right timing and depth, and both standard authorities decline the climate explanation anyway, Possehl for an internal ideological failure and Kenoyer for flooding routed through a crisis of legitimacy. Both attribute the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra to tectonic change rather than monsoon failure, which detaches the most-cited piece of hydrological evidence from the climate story altogether. @sec-appE sets the four readings against each other. On all of them, "de-urbanisation" fits better than "collapse".^[**Sources:** Possehl, *The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective* (2002), for the rejection of environmental causation and the ideological reading; Kenoyer, *Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization* (1998), for flooding mediated by a crisis of legitimacy, and both for the tectonic account of the Sarasvati; Williams (loc 1194, 1197) on reduced river flow c.4500--4200 years ago and Mithen (loc 9959) on c.2000 BCE drought, both representing the climate reading these authorities argue against. **Read more:** Possehl (2002).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** — carnelian and etched-carnelian beads, ivory, hardwoods (teak), pearls, and lapis lazuli carried on and re-exported from further north. Cotton is deliberately left off this list: the Indus had the world's oldest cotton tradition, but no cuneiform record places cotton among the Meluhha goods and no textile survives to show it moving west.
- **Main imports** — silver, tin, wool, and oil and grain.
- **Export markets** — Mesopotamia (Sumer and Akkad), reached through the Gulf intermediaries Magan (Oman) and Dilmun (Bahrain).
- **Import sources** — the same Gulf route in reverse, with Dilmun and Magan as the entrepots through which Mesopotamian silver and the metals of the wider Near East passed back to the Indus.^[**Sources:** Dalrymple (Loc 1163, 1168) on the Meluhha trade goods and the Gulf route; Roy (p.20, p.27) on the Indus settlements and the long-run trade pattern; Mithen (Loc 9058) on the Indus cotton tradition. **Read more:** Dalrymple, *The Golden Road* (2024).]

:::

## Dilmun — the Gulf entrepot

Dilmun, centred on Bahrain, was the junction of the Gulf trade that linked the Indus world to Mesopotamia, at its height between about 2600 and 1700 BCE. The early third-millennium Dilmun of the cuneiform texts most likely lay in eastern Arabia, around Tarut; Bahrain itself shows little substantial settlement before about 2200 BCE. Goods moved up the Gulf in stages: the Indus (known to the Sumerians as Meluhha) supplied carnelian, ivory, hardwoods, lapis and etched beads; Magan, on the Oman side, supplied copper; and Dilmun sat in the middle, gathering these and passing them on into Sumer. Its position made it the natural meeting point between the seaborne traffic of the lower Gulf and the river cities at its head.^[**Sources:** Pearson (Ch.3); Frahm (Page 46). **Read more:** Pearson, *The Indian Ocean* (2003).]

The economic logic is the one the module returns to again and again. Dilmun produced little of what it traded. Its wealth came from controlling a chokepoint — re-exporting Indus and Magan goods into the Mesopotamian demand-core and taking a cut on the way through. Value was captured not by making the carnelian or smelting the copper but by sitting astride the route along which they had to pass. That is the bottleneck-and-toll pattern: whoever controls the narrow passage between a supplier and a hungry market can levy the difference, and the entrepot grows rich on other people's goods.^[**Sources:** Pearson (Ch.3); Kriwaczek (Page 49). **Read more:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015).]

Two things about Dilmun cut against what an entrepôt is supposed to look like. The first is that it
was not culturally derivative. Harriet Crawford's summary is that Dilmun's material culture owed
"remarkably little either to its immediate neighbours, or to the trading partners at either end of
the trade routes", and the seals make the point concretely: Dilmun used round stamp seals with its
own iconography, Mesopotamia used cylinder seals, the Indus used square stamps. Three partners in
one trading system, three different ways of sealing a transaction. A place that lived by
intermediation did not become a blend of the people it intermediated between.

The second is stranger and bears directly on an argument this chapter has been building. Dilmun was
in sustained contact with three literate civilisations — Mesopotamia, Susa and the Indus — and ran
exactly the kind of complex, repeated, long-distance transactions that writing is supposed to have
emerged to keep track of. Yet we do not know that it had a writing system, and no Dilmun script has
been identified. Crawford, invoking the same argument about the origins of cuneiform used earlier in
this chapter, finds it hard to believe that such canny operators managed without one, and allows
that the need may have been met in other ways. Either way the case is a useful check. If writing
came out of the need to track transactions, here is a society with the transactions and, so far as
anyone can show, without the writing.^[**Sources:** Crawford, *Dilmun and its Gulf Neighbours*
(Cambridge University Press, 1998), on the distinctiveness of Dilmun's material culture, the
contrast between round, cylinder and square seals across the three partners, and the absence of an
identified Dilmun script despite contact with three literate neighbours; the argument she invokes
about writing emerging to track economic transactions is Nissen's, used earlier in this chapter for
Uruk. **Read more:** Crawford (1998).]

Dilmun's position also shaped who did the sailing. Few vessels ran the whole route: Mesopotamian boats went as far as Magan, and later only as far as Dilmun, while the Harappans worked the eastern leg, so the middle of the chain was where the goods changed hands and the margin was taken. That is why the entrepot mattered more than its own production ever warranted. Reading the direction and the range of the ships, in the absence of prices, is one of the few ways this period allows of inferring who was active and who was being supplied.^[**Sources:** Ratnagar, *Encounters* (1981), on transshipment and the staged route; Pearson (Ch.3) on Dilmun's position. **Read more:** Ratnagar, *Encounters* (1981).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** — re-exported goods rather than home produce: Indus carnelian, ivory and hardwoods; Magan copper passed upstream into Sumer.
- **Main imports** — silver, wool, oil and grain coming down from Mesopotamia, plus the goods it held in transit.
- **Export markets** — the Mesopotamian cities at the head of the Gulf, above all the Sumerian demand-core.
- **Import sources** — Meluhha (the Indus) and Magan (Oman) below it on the route.^[**Sources:** Pearson (Ch.3); Frahm (Page 46). **Read more:** Pearson, *The Indian Ocean* (2003).]
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Mesopotamia and Uruk — the demand core

Mesopotamia was the period's most commercially central node, and Uruk was its showpiece.

The scale of what happened there is easier to grasp as a rate than as a size. Through the proto-urban centuries, settlements in the region seldom passed 20 hectares, and counters and stamp seals were enough to keep track of what they produced. Then, by the end of the Late Uruk period, Uruk expanded to at least 250 hectares, some 2.5 square kilometres, holding perhaps 40,000 to 50,000 people. Nissen puts the city at that size around 3300 BCE, at the close of the sequence rather than its opening. That is more than a twelvefold increase in built area, and the world had not seen anything like it. It rested on an organised hinterland, whose size is routinely overstated: the radii in circulation are limits on early states in general, or measurements of other cities, rather than of Uruk, and the tax share usually quoted is an inference from agrarian history at large rather than a figure from any Sumerian record. What can be said is that water changed the arithmetic. River transport extended the catchment for bulk goods enormously, which is why the alluvium's cities sat on watercourses.

Two cautions. These are reconstructions, and the specialists are more reticent than the synthesis — Emberling opens his own chapter with cities that "may have housed 50,000 people or more" and then declines to say what population *makes* a settlement a city at all, which is the harder question. And the southern alluvium was not the only place cities were forming: Tell Brak, 750 kilometres north, had reached about 130 hectares before 3500 BCE, so any account making southern irrigation the *cause* of Mesopotamian urbanism has a northern problem.^[**Sources:** Nissen, "Urbanization and the techniques of communication: the Mesopotamian city of Uruk during the fourth millennium BCE", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 3 (2015), pp. 113–30, on the growth from under 20 to at least 250 hectares and the population estimate; Scott, *Against the Grain* (2017), ch. 4 "Agro-ecology of the Early State", for Uruk's 250 hectares, the Postgate/Abu Salabikh hinterland calculation and the one-fifth grain levy, and ch. 6 "Fragility of the Early State" for the forty-eight-kilometre requisition radius and the transport logic behind it. (Cited by chapter: the held text is an EPUB without pagination. An earlier draft gave a "ring of perhaps twenty competing city-states"; that count appears in neither Scott nor Emberling and has been removed.) Emberling, "Mesopotamian cities and urban process, 3500-1600 BCE", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 3 (2015), pp. 253-78, at p. 253 for the 50,000 figure and p. 254 for his refusal to set a population threshold defining a city, and at p. 263 for the argument that markets, walls and temples cannot explain the rise of cities because they only developed fully later. Population figures per hectare are themselves a contested method here, as they are for Pataliputra in the next chapter: see Postgate, "How Many Sumerians per Hectare?", *Cambridge Archaeological Journal* 4 (1994). **Read more:** Nissen (2015).]

Growth on that scale had to be administered, and the administrative technology is what survives. Beveled-rim bowls, mould-made in the millions and mostly holding the same amount, imply a standard unit of measure and, on the usual reading, the issue of rations; the cylinder seal answered the same problem of keeping track of a large and stratified population. Writing came out of that effort. The earliest tablets did not represent spoken language at all and were, in Hans Nissen's phrase, barely more than an extension of the techniques of accounting. That writing was invented to do bookkeeping and only later learned to carry literature is one of the more useful things this period has to say about how economies build the tools they need.^[**Sources:** Nissen (2015), pp. 113–30, on the beveled-rim bowls as mass production with a standard capacity, the cylinder seal, and writing as an extension of accounting; Goetzmann (loc 561) and Frahm (Page 34) on the accounting tablets. **Read more:** Nissen (2015).]

The clearest window onto how that economy worked was textile manufacture. Uruk's state workshops are credited with as many as 9,000 women — on the order of a fifth of the whole city — spinning and weaving wool into cloth that the temple and palace then disbursed or traded.

That figure needs handling with care. It comes from Scott, who writes a few paragraphs later that reading such evidence back from the Ur III archives to the Uruk period "is highly questionable", and the archaic Uruk tablets are largely undeciphered administrative accounts that will not support a workforce headcount of that precision. An establishment of that size, fed and housed from central stores and producing on central account, looks like a command economy: goods flowed up to the institution as grain and wool, and back down as rations and finished cloth, in the redistributive pattern Karl Polanyi placed at the heart of the early Near East. Whether that was the whole story is the live debate. The same society also ran private loans, partnerships and price-sensitive long-distance ventures, which point to genuine market exchange alongside the palace ledger. Redistribution and market dealing coexisted, and the balance between them remains contested rather than settled.

Two cautions belong with that, and the first is chronological. The archives documenting administered redistribution most fully are not Uruk's but those of the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2100 BCE, more than a millennium later; Emberling treats the great collection-and-redistribution centres as an innovation of that empire rather than a feature of the first cities. Reading Ur III practice back onto Uruk is a common move and not a safe one. The second is that the strongest version of the redistributive case has already been walked back, on the evidence of the very archive it was built from. @sec-appE has both.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 1040) on the workshops and the Polanyi reading; Emberling, *CWH* vol. 3 (2015), pp. 253-78, at p. 261 on the redistributive model requiring revision, p. 262 on the temple-city model and the Ba'u archive, p. 263 on markets, walls and temples as late developments, and pp. 272, 275 on collection and redistribution as an Ur III innovation. **Read more:** Emberling (2015).]

Money and credit were already mature, well before any coin was struck. Silver and barley served as units of account and means of payment, so prices existed even though coinage did not. Interest-bearing debt is securely attested from the later third millennium and may reach back to around 3000 BCE; the rates were later codified under Hammurabi at 20 per cent on silver and 33 1/3 per cent on barley. Debt could spiral into bondage, and rulers periodically wiped the slate: in about 2400 BCE Enmetena of Lagash declared *amargi*, "freedom", cancelling debts — the first recorded use of the word in a political document. Credit belonged to this economy from the start. What arrived later was minted coinage, and the continuous price series that came with it.^[**Sources:** Graeber (Loc 8075, 4560); Goetzmann (loc 592, 836, 838); Kriwaczek (Page 101). **Read more:** Graeber, *Debt: The First 5,000 Years* (2011).]

What made Mesopotamia the demand pole was its geology. The southern alluvium was rich in silt and grain but had almost no metal, building stone or timber of its own, so the materials of an urban civilisation had to be imported. Even Uruk's monumental architecture leaned on stone hauled some eighty kilometres, and the metals, hard stones and fine woods came from much further. An integrated trading sphere — the "Uruk world system" — already linked the Iranian plateau to the eastern Mediterranean between about 3500 and 3100 BCE, then contracted around 3000 BCE as the long-distance networks thinned and an era of warring city-states began. The luxuries it had carried travelled astonishing distances: lapis lazuli from Badakhshan in Afghanistan moved roughly 2,500 kilometres to reach Mesopotamia, and onward to Egypt. The resource-poor core, in other words, generated the demand that pulled goods across half a continent.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 1199); Kriwaczek (Page 40, 49, 72); Frahm (Page 46). **Read more:** Kriwaczek, *Babylon* (2010).]

The mechanics of that import trade are best seen in the early second-millennium tin caravans between Assur and the Anatolian colony at Kanesh. Donkey trains of fifty or more animals carried tin and textiles roughly 950 kilometres on a journey of about fifty days, exchanging them for silver.

The price gap was the point. Quoted in silver, which served as the period's unit of account, 100 shekels of tin cost about 6.7 shekels of silver at Assur, about 10 at Mari, and about 14.3 in Anatolia, where tin was scarcer and dearer; the textiles fetched three to four times their Assyrian price. Merchants reckoned gross mark-ups near 100 per cent on the metal and 200 per cent on the cloth. Those are mark-ups and not profits: the fifty-day journey, the fodder, the drivers, the tolls, the agent's commission and something like a hundred days of tied-up capital all came out of them first. Nor is this arbitrage, which is riskless and simultaneous; it is a capital-committing venture across fifty days and 950 kilometres, and the returns had to compensate the risk or nobody would have gone.

That price gap is the most useful number the period yields. Tin cost roughly twice as much in Anatolia as at Assur, and the gap persisted for generations while tonnages moved along the route.

A gap that stable is not a market failing to integrate. It is the cost of integration, quoted: what it took to put a shekel of tin 950 kilometres further west, in donkeys, drivers, fodder, tolls, protection and time. Read that way, Assur and Kanesh were about as integrated as the technology of the day allowed, and the measure of later integration is not that such gaps disappear but that they shrink toward the physical cost of carriage. That is the same test the rest of this book applies to grain in the nineteenth century and to containers in the twentieth, run on the only evidence the Bronze Age left. To the south-east, a separate maritime arm ran down the Gulf: Sumer drew copper from Magan (Oman) and exotic goods from Meluhha (the Indus), traded through the entrepot of Dilmun (Bahrain), with one Ur merchant, Ea-nasir, assembling fifty-one investors for a single Dilmun venture. Tin, copper, lapis and carnelian flowed in; the demand core sat at the western end of the longest exchange networks of the age.^[**Sources:** Frahm (Page 47, 48); Kriwaczek (Page 215, 216, 49); Goetzmann (loc 940). **Read more:** Frahm, *Assyria* (2023).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** — silver and barley (also serving as money and units of account); woollen textiles from the state workshops; grain and other agricultural surplus of the irrigated alluvium.
- **Main imports** — the materials the alluvium lacked: tin and copper for bronze, building stone and timber, and high-value luxuries (lapis lazuli, carnelian, ivory, hardwoods).
- **Export markets** — Anatolia (textiles and silver through Kanesh); the Gulf trade with Magan and the Indus via the Dilmun entrepot; the wider Uruk-system sphere from the Iranian plateau to the eastern Mediterranean.
- **Import sources** — Anatolia and the eastern highlands (metals, silver); Badakhshan (lapis, ~2,500 km away); Magan/Oman (copper) and Meluhha/the Indus (carnelian, ivory, hardwoods) through Dilmun.^[**Sources:** Frahm (Page 46, 47, 48); Kriwaczek (Page 40, 49, 215); Scott (Page 1199). **Read more:** Kriwaczek, *Babylon* (2010).]

:::

![The Great Ziggurat of Ur, built under the Third Dynasty of Ur around 2100 BCE --- the temple-and-palace institution that pulled metal and stone across half a continent. Note the date: the administered redistribution best documented in Mesopotamia belongs to this Ur III period, more than a millennium after Uruk, and Geoff Emberling treats it as an Ur III innovation rather than a feature of early cities. Photo: U.S. DoD (Cherie A. Thurlby), public domain.](book/figures/photos/ziggurat-ur.jpg){#fig-ziggurat width=72%}

![Mesopotamia and Uruk as the demand core: a resource-poor alluvium importing tin, copper, lapis and carnelian along the Assur--Kanesh caravan route and down the Gulf through Dilmun, against exports of silver, barley and woollen cloth (stylised; not to scale). Author's schematic.](book/figures/map-mesopotamia-01.png){#fig-mapmeso01 width=85%}

Even that figure is a construction rather than an observation. Adams put the region's urbanised share at as much as 78 per cent across Sumer around 2400 BCE, while his own survey figures for Ur III Umma implied nearer 25; Steinkeller, working from the place-names in the administrative texts rather than from surface survey, put 70 to 80 per cent of Umma's people outside the city. Neither is careless, and the gap between them is mostly a gap between methods — though not wholly, since the two estimates also cover different places and different centuries — the derivation is set out in @sec-appD.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Egypt — the Nile apart

Egypt was a riverine core of the first rank, but it stood largely outside the Gulf system that linked the Indus to Mesopotamia. Its wealth came from the Nile: a narrow ribbon of irrigated land whose predictable flood underwrote dense agriculture and a centralised state from unification around 3100 BCE, and through the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms from about 2686 — with the two Intermediate Periods as genuine interruptions to that centralisation rather than footnotes to it. Early Dynastic Egypt matters here for a further reason: it is the state contemporary with Uruk, and the period of the documented Egyptian contacts with the Uruk world. Where Mesopotamia depended on uncertain rainfall and rivers, Egypt's annual inundation gave it an agrarian base reliable enough to sustain monumental building and a deep bureaucracy, a precocious complexity to rival anything in the Near East.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 1064, 1076); Cline (loc 505). **Read more:** Scott, *Against the Grain* (2017).]

Egypt traded, but along its own axes rather than through the Gulf. It looked south to Punt for incense, ivory and exotic goods, and east through the Sinai and the Red Sea margins for copper, turquoise and contact with the Levant. Lapis lazuli from Afghanistan reached Egypt by overland relay, a reminder that it was tied into the wider Bronze Age web at the edges. But its trading face pointed down the Nile corridor and across the Sinai land bridge, not down the Persian Gulf, and the Indus-to-Sumer relay ran without it.^[**Sources:** Frahm (Page 46); Kriwaczek (Page 49). **Read more:** Cline, *1177 B.C.* (2014).]

Where Egypt put its surplus is the more interesting question, and the answer is not "into cities". John Baines argues that the values of early Egyptian rulers and elites seem not to have focused on cities at all. Power was presented across a landscape rather than concentrated in an urban form: dispersed mortuary monuments and necropolis sites, movement between them, and a careful interplay of display and concealment. Egyptian cities were distinctive in layout, constrained by the floodplain and overshadowed by those monuments, and it was only later, by the New Kingdom, that the society became more city-focused and its cities came to resemble those elsewhere in the Near East.

Set that beside the other two riverine cores and this chapter has a comparison worth making. Three societies of roughly the same era each generated a large agricultural surplus, and each put it somewhere different. Uruk put it into the city itself and into the apparatus for running one: walls, workshops, ration bowls turned out in the millions, and the accounting that became writing. The Harappans put it into infrastructure that nobody signed, with the seals that recorded claims on resources sitting in ordinary households rather than in palaces. Egypt put it into monuments to named individuals, spread along a river. None of these is a market economy, and the differences between them are not differences of wealth. They are differences in who could command the surplus and what they wanted it for, which is a question this book asks in every later chapter with better data and rarely a clearer contrast.^[**Sources:** Baines, "Ancient Egyptian cities: monumentality and performance", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 3 (2015), pp. 27-47, at pp. 44-45, on elite values not focused on cities, the distribution of power across the landscape, and the later New Kingdom shift; Nissen (2015) and Green (2022) for the Uruk and Harappan comparisons drawn above. **Read more:** Baines (2015).]

There is a further reason to keep Egypt in this chapter rather than filing it as a magnificent
irrelevance, and it comes from the economics of its record-keeping. Brian Muhs argues that the
Egyptian state expanded the use of writing over three millennia for a straightforward fiscal reason:
to document and exact taxes more efficiently, and so to run redistribution better. But the writing
did something its promoters did not intend. Once titles and transfers could be documented and
enforced, the cost of making a private transaction fell relative to the cost of going through the
institution, and private exchange grew at redistribution's expense. Silver, coming into use as a
common measure of value and store of wealth, lowered those costs again for high-value dealings. The
state then began taxing transfers in silver, which gave it a direct fiscal interest in documenting
and enforcing private property rights still further.

That loop runs through the rest of this book. An administrative
technology adopted to make extraction work better ended up lowering the transaction costs of the
private exchange that competed with extraction, and the state's own revenue interest then pushed it
into underwriting the competition. It is the same insight economists reach for when they ask why
some activity happens inside an organisation and some through a market, and Egypt supplies a
three-thousand-year run of it. Set beside Uruk, where writing began as accounting and stayed
institutional for a very long time, and beside the Phoenician alphabet later in this chapter, which
put writing in a merchant's hands, the point is that the same technology can push an economy in
opposite directions depending on who can afford it and what the state wants from it.^[**Sources:**
Muhs, *The Ancient Egyptian Economy, 3000-30 BCE* (Cambridge University Press, 2016), whose central
argument this paragraph follows: writing expanded for fiscal reasons, then lowered the transaction
costs of private property transfers relative to redistribution, with silver as a unified measure of
value lowering them again and giving the state an incentive to document and enforce private titles.
Muhs frames the book explicitly in New Institutional Economics terms, and the organisation-versus-
market question is Coase's. **Read more:** Muhs (2016).]

So Egypt is best read as precocious but separate: an early, rich, highly organised state that developed in parallel with the Gulf system rather than as part of it. It mattered enormously in the later eastern-Mediterranean world — by the fourteenth century BCE its correspondence with Hatti, Babylon and the Aegean shows it deep in the palace-economy network whose collapse around 1177 BCE it barely survived. For the first integration of the Gulf, though, it is a neighbouring core, not a participant.^[**Sources:** Cline (2014), ch. 2, on Egypt's correspondence with Hatti, Babylon and the Aegean in the Amarna archive. **Read more:** Cline (2014).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** — Nile agricultural surplus and manufactured goods; gold from the eastern deserts and Nubia.
- **Main imports** — incense and ivory from Punt; copper and turquoise from Sinai; lapis from Afghanistan by overland relay.
- **Export markets** — the Levant and, increasingly, the eastern-Mediterranean palace world.
- **Import sources** — Punt to the south, Sinai and the Red Sea to the east, the Levant to the north-east.^[**Sources:** Cline (loc 505, 1065); Frahm (Page 46). **Read more:** Cline, *1177 B.C.* (2014).]
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The steppe — the dynamic engine

The Eurasian steppe was no periphery but the era's main artery: an unbroken grass corridor running some 7,000 km from eastern Europe to the Great Wall of China. What turned this ribbon of grass into a power-and-information highway was the horse. A herder on foot could manage about 200 sheep; mounted, the same herder could manage some 500, ranging 50 to 60 kilometres in a working day around them. Read that figure carefully: it is a herdsman's daily range, not the pace of a migration. Households moving with their animals covered something closer to 10 to 20 kilometres on a day they moved, and nearer nine or ten averaged across a whole migration, held to the speed of the herd and to the grass it had to stop and eat. What mounted herding bought was reach, and reach is what made the corridor the fastest channel for moving people, animals and news across the continent.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015), p. 77, for the 200-to-500 herding gain and the 50-60 km working range, and p. 17 for a rider's daily distance. **Note on a figure clarified:** Cunliffe's sentence makes the herdsman, not the flock, the thing covering 50-60 km; earlier drafts of this chapter read it as a migration rate. Cunliffe gives no source for the number, and it should be treated as an authorial assertion. **Read more:** Cunliffe (2015).]

A cluster of innovations compounded the advantage. The wheel, and then the chariot — the earliest known examples of which come from Sintashta graves in the Urals, before 2000 BCE — spread outward along the grass, reaching the Near East by the nineteenth century BCE and China only around 1200 BCE. Alongside these ran what Andrew Sherratt called a "secondary-products revolution": the use of animals for traction, wool and dairy rather than meat alone. That thesis is contested — whether it was a single fourth-millennium event or a gradual, patchy adoption is debated — but the underlying shift, animals exploited while alive, was real and it multiplied what a pastoral economy could yield.^[**Sources:** Anthony (loc 6171); Cunliffe (loc 1266). **Read more:** Anthony, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* (2007).]

The corridor was also a vector of migration. The Yamnaya expansion out of the Pontic-Caspian steppe around 3000 BCE has been associated, on present ancient-DNA readings, with a large influx of steppe-derived ancestry into Europe — as much as 90 per cent of the gene pool in Britain at the Bell Beaker transition around 2450 BCE, and about 75 per cent in Corded Ware burials in Germany, rather than a single figure for the continent — a striking figure that should be held cautiously, since the genetics and its demographic interpretation are still moving. The steppe, then, was a channel and an engine at once: it raided the settled cores, traded with them, and at times poured into them, shaping the riverine worlds it bordered rather than merely lying beyond them.^[**Sources:** Olalde et al., *Nature* 555 (2018), for the British figure and Haak et al., *Nature* 522 (2015), for Corded Ware Germany; Spinney (Loc 754, 1338); Anthony (loc 5149). An earlier draft gave "up to roughly 90 per cent of Europe's gene pool", which takes the highest regional number and generalises it. **Read more:** Anthony, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* (2007).]

**Trade profile**

- **Main exports** — horses, mounted mobility, and metal-working skill; above all the capacity to move goods, people and force at speed.
- **Main imports** — grain, textiles and finished metalwork drawn from the settled cores.
- **Export markets** — the riverine cores it raided, traded with and migrated into, from Mesopotamia to the forming East Asian core.
- **Import sources** — the same settled cores, supplying the agricultural and manufactured goods the grassland could not produce.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe (loc 158, 909); Anthony (loc 6171). **Read more:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015).]
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## How we know
This period leaves no price series at all, and that single absence governs everything the chapter can claim. The test the book uses from @sec-ch08 onward — a price gap bounded by the cost of carriage, narrowing as that cost falls — can barely be run here. What the period does leave, in the Assyrian merchant archives, is a handful of exchange ratios at either end of one route, and those turn out to be more useful than they look. Everything else has to be read archaeologically, from the diffusion of goods and shared standards: an Indus seal in a Mesopotamian layer, a set of Harappan weights, a string of etched carnelian beads in a Sumerian grave. Each is a physical trace that two distant economies had touched. None of them says how much, how often, or at what price. And the record is biased the way the introduction warns: organic things rotted in the monsoon tropics and survived in dry Egypt and cool Europe, so what we have systematically under-documents the ocean world this book centres on.

*Sources: on reading integration by the diffusion of goods, and the Indus weights, seals and carnelian beads in Mesopotamia, Frahm (Page 46); on the Meluhhan ships and interpreter and the survival bias, Cunliffe (Loc 158). Read more: Cunliffe, By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean (2015).*
:::

## The period on its own terms

Before the cycles, a word about what the base cost. Every economy in this chapter stood on farming, and farming was not obviously a bargain for the people who did it.

The skeletal record across the agricultural transition, read at sites worldwide, mostly shows the same direction of travel: shorter stature, more dental caries as fermentable carbohydrates displaced a mixed forager diet, more enamel defects from childhood stress, and heavier loads of infectious disease as people settled at density alongside their animals and their refuse. Sedentism brought contaminated water, vermin, poor sanitation, harvest failure and soil exhaustion, and it narrowed the variety of what was eaten. Social inequality appears alongside all of this. The finding is not universal, and bioarchaeologists are careful about it, since any one skeletal marker can have several causes and a minority of studies run the other way. But the broad pattern is the physical counterpart of the Malthusian result set out at the end of this chapter: the gains from better technology and better land went into more people rather than into better-fed ones. Agriculture was a way of supporting numbers, not a way of living well, and that is the yardstick this book carries forward.^[**Sources:** Roberts, "What did agriculture do for us? The bioarchaeology of health and diet", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 2 (2015), pp. 93–123, on stature, dental caries, enamel hypoplasia, infectious disease loads and the living conditions of settled communities, and on the studies that do not follow the trend. The econometric counterpart is Ashraf and Galor (2011), discussed at the end of this chapter. **Read more:** Roberts (2015).]

The period ran not as one smooth arc but as a sequence of integrations that rose and then came apart, three times over, on a stage that geology had set tens of millions of years before the first city. The three cycles are worth naming at the outset, because the shape returns in every later chapter. An early Uruk sphere reached from the Iranian plateau to the Mediterranean and then contracted. The Gulf trade that the Harappans ran followed it, and ended with their cities. Then the Late Bronze Age system of the eastern Mediterranean, the tightest of the three, broke the hardest. Between the second and the third sits a gap of some three centuries that no trading cycle fills, and what carried that gap was a technology rather than a trade: the horse, the wheel and the chariot, remaking on the steppe what movement cost.

![Three thousand years in three cycles, not one arc: an early Uruk world system rises and contracts, the Gulf trade the Harappans ran follows and ends with their cities c.1900 BCE, and after a gap that the steppe technologies carry, the Late Bronze Age system rises and collapses c.1177 BCE, before the reset by 500 BCE. Drawn to a linear time axis, so the long interval between cycles two and three is real time rather than spacing. Author's schematic.](book/figures/phase-cycles-01.png){#fig-cycles01 width=92%}

**Deep time: the stage is built.** The board was assembled long before there was anything on it to call an economy. The collision that raised the Himalayas organised the climate of half the world, and the section above has already set out what it produced: the reversing monsoon, the river basins that fed the first surplus-producing societies, and the three corridors that carry goods for the rest of this book. What matters for the narrative is the tension the geography left behind. The same monsoon that made predictable round-trip voyaging possible could, when it weakened, help hollow out a civilisation, and both of its faces appear in the cycles below. The determinism is real but bounded: deep structures shaped what could happen, and people still chose the moves — a caution worth holding against the harder geographic readings of Cunliffe and, before him, Diamond.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe (Loc 158); Pearson (Ch.1). **Read more:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015).]

**Cycle one: the first integration, and its contraction (c.3500–3000 BCE).** The earliest integrated trading sphere the record shows did not run through the Gulf at all, but overland across the northern Near East. From roughly 3500 to 3100 BCE a "Uruk world system" linked the Iranian plateau to the eastern Mediterranean, drawing distant materials toward the Mesopotamian alluvium where the world's first true cities were rising. Uruk itself was already a demand-core of startling size: by around 3300 BCE it covered some 250 hectares and held perhaps forty to fifty thousand people. That is a settled area rather than an intramural one: Uruk's wall belongs to the Early Dynastic period, four centuries later. Its state textile workshops are credited with as many as nine thousand women, on the order of a fifth of the city, subject to the caution entered above.

Such a place pulled goods from far away.

Lapis lazuli from the mines of Badakhshan in north-eastern Afghanistan travelled roughly 2,500 kilometres to reach Mesopotamia, and the same blue stone reached Egypt at roughly the same period. This was integration in its archaic form, measurable not by prices but by the diffusion of materials far from their sources.

Then it came apart. Around 3000 BCE the Uruk system contracted: the long-distance exchange network thinned and an era of warring city-states opened in its place. Lapis itself kept coming — the greatest concentration of it outside Afghanistan is the Royal Cemetery of Ur, five centuries after the supposed break — so what changed was the scale and the politics of the traffic rather than its existence. The period's first paired peak-and-fall therefore happened before the Gulf trade that the older accounts foreground, which means the integration-then-disintegration rhythm that defines this whole story began one cycle earlier than is often assumed.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 1199, 805, 1040); Kriwaczek (Page 49, 72); Frahm (Page 34). **Read more:** Scott, *Against the Grain* (2017).]

**Cycle two: the Gulf trade, and the Harappans led it (c.2600--1900 BCE).** As the overland system frayed, a maritime one took its place along the Gulf.

From about 2600 BCE a sea trade linked the Indus cities --- Meluhha to the Sumerians --- to Mesopotamia through Magan on the Oman peninsula and Dilmun, the entrepot on Bahrain where goods were trans-shipped. The Indus profile above sets out what moved and which way; what matters for the sequence is that agency here was not a fixed property of either side. Through the mature phase the initiative ran west. Later, once Harappan ports on the Makran coast could be reached without crossing open-ocean monsoon water, the carrying passed increasingly to Mesopotamians and Dilmunites. The value sat, as it will so often in this book, with neither producer nor consumer but with whoever held the chokepoint: Dilmun took a cut on goods it never made. One qualification on the end of this cycle, because it is usually got wrong. What stopped around 1900 BCE was Indus participation, not the Gulf system --- Dilmun's commerce with Mesopotamia ran on through the Isin-Larsa and Old Babylonian periods and revived again under the Kassites. The network survived the loss of its eastern terminus by re-sourcing.^[**Sources:** Kriwaczek (Page 49); Scott (Page 1551). **Read more:** Ratnagar, *Encounters* (1981).]

**Cycle two ends: the Harappan cities empty (c.1900 BCE).** The mature urban phase gave way to de-urbanisation and an eastward shift of population, and the great planned cities lost the density that had defined them. The Indus profile above gives the debate in full; three things belong in the sequence. The de-urbanisation was broadly coincident with the 4.2 ka event --- but 4.2 ka is around 2200 BCE, three centuries earlier, which is a long time for a cause to take effect. The palaeoclimate record does not show the sharp, sustained drought a mono-causal climate story would need. And "collapse" is the wrong word for what happened: the cities went, the people did not.^[**Sources:** Williams (Loc 1194); Mohan (Loc 531) on the end of the urban phase c.1900 BCE. Staubwasser and Gupta et al. for the abrupt-forcing reading, Giosan et al. for gradual hydrological change, Possehl for multi-causal social transformation. **Read more:** Possehl, *The Indus Civilization* (2002).]

The word "collapse" is the wrong one here, and the languages are what show it. The cities went; the people did not. Steppe-derived ancestry entered South Asia between about 2000 and 1500 BCE, and the core of the *Rig Veda* is conventionally placed between about 1500 and 1200 BCE. Keep the genetic and the linguistic evidence distinct: an individual from Rakhigarhi, sequenced in 2019, carried no steppe ancestry at all, so whatever arrived did not arrive early enough to be Harappan. Separately, and from the other direction, a migration out of China after 2000 BCE brought Austroasiatic speech and a new variety of rice in from the east. Present-day Indian languages still carry that layering — a Dravidian population formed long before, an Indo-Aryan layer arriving after the cities emptied, an Austroasiatic layer from the east — so the movement that the archaeology only gestures at is legible in how the descendants of those people speak. It is a reminder worth carrying: when the material record thins, other records sometimes do not.^[**Sources:** Narasimhan et al., "The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia", *Science* 365 (2019), for the 2000--1500 BCE window on steppe-derived ancestry; Shinde et al., *Cell* 179 (2019), for the Rakhigarhi genome; Mohan (Loc 531, 649, 3292) on the end of the urban phase, the influx, and the Austroasiatic migration and rice after 2000 BCE. **Note on dates corrected:** an earlier draft placed the Arya at 1700 BCE and the *Rig Veda*'s composition with them, both following Mohan; neither sits inside the consensus range, and this is contested and politically charged ground on which a textbook should be more careful than usual, not less. **Read more:** Narasimhan et al. (2019).]

**Between the cycles: the steppe remade what movement cost.** The Harappan cities emptied around 1900 BCE, and the eastern Mediterranean system that follows did not come together until the sixteenth century. What fills it is usually said to be a technology rather than a trading cycle, and the technology is real enough — it came from the great grass corridor to the north of every core in this chapter.

But the claim that no trading system occupies the interval will not survive a look at this chapter's own evidence.

The Assyrian tin trade between Assur and Kanesh ran from about 1950 to 1750 BCE, squarely inside it, and it is the best-documented commercial network anywhere in these three thousand years: the price ratios, the caravan logistics, the credit and the merchant families all come from there. The Mari archives and the Old Babylonian Gulf trade sit in the same window. What the interval lacks is not commerce but a *maritime* cycle of the kind that brackets it — and the Assyrian material is vivid because a merchant quarter's private papers happened to survive, which is a fact about archives rather than about the economy.

Read the three cycles, then, as three horizons of surviving evidence that coincide with three real expansions, not as an account of when trade did and did not happen.

What the interval does carry, and the bracketing cycles do not, is a change in what movement cost. The steppe profile above sets out the technology; the point to take forward is its pace.

The domestic horse lineage that spread across Eurasia expands only from about 2200 BCE, which makes horse and chariot near-contemporaries; and the earliest known chariots, from Sintashta graves east of the Urals before 2000 BCE, reached the Near East within a century or two and China only around 1200. Nine hundred years for one technology to cross a continent is the diffusion speed of this world, and it is the baseline against which every later chapter's should be read.^[**Sources:** Librado et al., "The origins and spread of domestic horses from the Western Eurasian steppes", *Nature* 598 (2021), for the DOM2 lineage and its expansion from c.2200 BCE, and Outram et al., *Science* 323 (2009), for Botai horses belonging to the Przewalski rather than the domestic line; Cunliffe (Loc 158, 909, 1266); Anthony (Loc 6171). **Note on a date corrected:** earlier drafts gave domestication at c.4800 BCE, which is Anthony's 2007 position and has since been substantially revised, by Anthony's own acknowledgement. **Read more:** Librado et al. (2021).]

What riding did to the economy shows up in two things, and only one of them is a speed.

The first is scale. A herder on foot managed perhaps two hundred animals; mounted, he could hold around five hundred and graze the deep interior. That is a productivity gain of roughly 150 per cent, in the ordinary sense of the term.

The second is reach, which is not the same thing as speed, and the difference is where the usual story goes wrong. Daily rates barely moved: a household travelling with its herds made 10 to 20 kilometres on a day it moved at all, a party on foot 18 to 25, a rider travelling light 30 to 45.

The herding figure flatters it further, because the migration was itself the grazing. Kazakh auls covering 800 to 1,000 kilometres took 90 to 110 days over some seventy halts --- a net advance of nine or ten kilometres a day. A Lorestan tribe's ninety-kilometre move was reckoned a ten-day trek. Nine to eleven kilometres a day turns up in region after region.

So moving with animals was slower than walking, and riding roughly doubled a traveller's pace rather than transforming it.

What changed by an order of magnitude was range. Anthony's Yamnaya herders moved within an annual orbit of under 50 kilometres, while mounted raiding parties struck hundreds of kilometres out and drove livestock home. The economy's orbit stayed small. The reach of force and information did not.

That separation is the thing to carry forward, because the two never rejoin. The spectacular courier speeds this period is often credited with --- the Persian road, the Roman post, the Mongol relay --- belong to later societies that built stations and kept remounts at them. The Venetian letter, the telegraph and the container ship are all later chapters of the same story.

Two distinctions inside the word "nomad" matter here. Ingold's is between living off a dead animal and living off a live one: milk, blood and wool are a renewable yield where meat is terminal, and the move to secondary products is what turns a herd from a larder into an income.

The second is a warning against reading any of this as environmental destiny. Specialist pastoralism tends to dominate where other farming cannot succeed. But the forest steppes of southern Russia and northern Kazakhstan grow wheat without irrigation today, and were held by herders from the Eneolithic to the twentieth century anyway. Farming was possible there. Herders kept the ground for two thousand years regardless.

Hold that against this chapter's closing debate on how much weight geography should carry.^[**Sources:** Outram, "Pastoralism", in *The Cambridge World History*, vol. 2 (2015), pp. 161-85, for Ingold's four modes, the primary and secondary products distinction, and the forest-steppe counter-case that warns against simple environmental determinism. **Read more:** Outram (2015).]

The consequences ran outward from there. Bigger herds needed more land, land meant conflict, conflict meant alliances, and alliances were bought with elite goods — so long-distance exchange was partly a by-product of horsemanship. These tools also powered the Indo-European expansions that reshaped the genetic and linguistic map of Eurasia, though the migration-and-linguistics detail is contested terrain and best treated lightly. The steppe was no periphery in this period; it was the era's dynamic engine.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015), p. 77, on the herd-size gain from mounted herding — not Anthony, who is the source this note goes on to withdraw for the travel rates, and the same misattribution had reached this figure too. **Note on figures corrected:** earlier drafts gave three daily travel rates (ten to thirty kilometres on foot, fifty to sixty driving herds, a hundred to a hundred and fifty riding light) and cited Anthony among the sources. None of the three appears anywhere in his book, and the rates given above replace them: households with herds 10-20 km on a moving day and 9-11 km/day of net advance across a migration (Kartaeva, *bilig* 90, 2019, on Kazakh seasonal migration -- 800-1,000 km in 90-110 days with some seventy halts; Tawfiq, "'Asayer", *Encyclopaedia Iranica* II/7, giving a Bala Geriva move of 90 km as a ten-day trek; Barth, *Nomads of South Persia*, 1961; and the American cattle drives in McCoy 1874, which run 16-24 on a moving day but 13-14 door-to-door), foot travel 18-25 (Herodotus 5.53 at 27.8 on the Royal Road; Clausewitz's one-third rest-day discount; every documented transcontinental walker below 20), and a light rider 30-45 (US *Cavalry Drill Regulations*, 1916, pp. 387-88, at 40 km per marching day). The 100-150 figure is a two-to-four-day forced march or a relay rate, not a sustained one. Denis Sinor, "Horse and Pasture in Inner Asian History", *Oriens Extremus* 19 (1972), sets out the grazing arithmetic that caps herd movement. Cunliffe (Loc 909, 1266) and Spinney (Loc 754) on the wider consequences. **Read more:** Anthony (2007).]

**Cycle three: the Late Bronze Age was already an age of globalisation.** By the fourteenth century BCE the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East ran as one working system. Egypt, Hatti, Babylonia, Assyria, Mittani, Mycenaean Greece, Cyprus — the Alashiya of the records, a metal-rich island famous for its copper — and the Syrian port of Ugarit were all in sustained contact with each other.

Their post survives.

The Amarna letters, some 350 letters, from a corpus of 382 tablets, written between about 1365 and 1335 BCE, carry correspondence reaching from Nubia to the Aegean to Iran, and they are written in Akkadian, the diplomatic lingua franca of the day, which almost none of the senders spoke at home. A shared script, a shared protocol and a shared honorific vocabulary — kings addressed one another as "my brother" — are together the strongest single indicator of system-hood that the period offers.

Specialisation was visible in what moved: Cypriot copper, Nubian gold, Afghan lapis, Baltic amber in Mycenaean graves. Hittite iron belongs on a different list — rare, prestigious, and known largely from a single royal letter about a dagger blade, it was not a traded commodity in the way the others were.

The system had rules, too.
