Its conflicts were wars of readjustment rather than annihilation, and its kings married each other's daughters, complained in writing about late consignments of gold, and went on trading. What that correspondence describes is trade wearing court dress: royal "gifts" carried explicit reciprocity, stated weights and complaints about quality, and the line between gift-exchange and commerce is one worth refusing to draw too sharply. Cline calls the result a golden age of internationalism, and puts the globalised economy that defined it at three hundred years and more.^[**Sources:** Cline (2014), prologue on Alashiya and Cypriot copper, chs. 1-2 on Akkadian as the diplomatic language and on the "Golden Age" of internationalism and globalization, (Loc 2260) on three centuries of globalised economy, (Loc 3810) on the first great international era. **Read more:** Cline, *1177 B.C.* (2014).]

The physical counterpart of that correspondence is a single hull. The Uluburun ship went down off the Anatolian coast in the late fourteenth century BCE, conventionally around 1300 and on some recent readings nearer 1320, carrying roughly ten tonnes of copper as 354 four-cornered "oxhide" ingots and 121 bun-shaped ones, along with an estimated tonne of tin. That is close to the ten-to-one ratio bronze requires, so the cargo was a bronze industry in kit form, about eleven tonnes of alloy waiting to be made. Around it lay some 175 glass ingots in cobalt blue, turquoise and lavender, a tonne of terebinth resin in Canaanite jars, African ebony, elephant tusks and hippopotamus teeth, Baltic amber, Mesopotamian bitumen, and 135 pieces of Cypriot pottery. The excavator counts products of at least nine or ten cultures aboard.

Two things about that hull matter more than the inventory.

The first is when it sank. The ship is easily filed under the collapse it actually precedes by roughly 120 years: it dates the system at its height, not its unravelling.

The second is what kind of voyage it was, and here the chapter should not get ahead of the evidence. The wreck carried gold cups of a type kings sent one another as diplomatic gifts, and a cargo whose components — ivory, ebony, glass, worked gold — are the very goods the Amarna letters list as royal presents; its 354 oxhide ingots amount to something like 325 talents of copper, against shipments of 100 and 200 talents that those letters record passing between courts. Cemal Pulak, who excavated it, reads the ship as an official dispatch rather than a merchant venture. But it also carried several sets of pan-balance weights on the Syrian shekel of about 9.3 grams, the working tools of perhaps three merchants, and copper ingots of varying weight that had to be weighed at each transaction. His own conclusion is that an official carried the king's goods and did some private trading on the side. For an economics textbook that is the finding rather than the caveat: administered court-to-court exchange and weighed, priced, transaction-by-transaction commerce were running in the same hold.^[**Sources:** Pulak, "The Uluburun shipwreck: an overview", *International Journal of Nautical Archaeology* 27 (1998), pp. 188, 193, 199, 201-2, 204, 209-10, 214-15, 219-20. The date rests on a tree-ring reading giving a last observable ring at 1305 BCE, with the ship sinking after that but probably not much later; note that the absolute anchoring of the Aegean dendrochronology was explicitly provisional in 1998 and has been revisited since, so the year should be treated as approximate. Cline (2014), ch. 2, on the ship as a microcosm of international contact. **Read more:** Pulak (1998).]

**Cycle three ends: the Collapse (c.1177 BCE).** Then the densely interconnected palace economies of the eastern Mediterranean failed together, and they failed as a system.

Their dependence on long-distance metal shows the exposure plainly: bronze needed tin, tin sat almost nowhere near the cities that used it, so it had to travel, and its role, as Carol Bell put it, was probably not far different from crude oil's today.

When the web tore around 1177 BCE the cost was systemic.

Mainland Greece may have lost forty to sixty per cent of its people, falling from perhaps six hundred thousand to around three hundred and thirty thousand, and Babylonia possibly as much as three-quarters before any recovery. Ugarit, destroyed around 1190 BCE, saw some eight thousand inhabitants flee and was not reoccupied for roughly six hundred and fifty years.

The collapse was over-determined — earthquake swarm, drought, the movements conventionally called the Sea Peoples, internal rebellion, the cutting of the trade routes — and that is precisely Cline's argument: once a system is this tightly coupled, no single cause is needed.

The Sea Peoples in particular need handling with care. Cline calls them a convenient scapegoat, a construct assembled by nineteenth-century scholarship, and the tide has turned against reading them as the agent of the collapse rather than one of its symptoms.

This was integration's first systemic failure, and its lesson, inherited by the whole module, is that a tightly connected system can break in a way a loose one cannot. What followed is the subject of the next section, and it took seven centuries. ^[**Sources:** Cline, *1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed* (2014), ch. 4 for the destruction of Ugarit and the flight of some eight thousand inhabitants, and ch. 5 for the over-determined, systems-collapse reading of the causes. Cited by chapter: the held edition is an EPUB without pagination. **Read more:** Cline (2014).]

## After the collapse: the Phoenician centuries, c. 1177--500 BCE

The wreckage took a long time to clear, and what replaced the palaces did not look like them. Iron
changed the metals arithmetic, because iron ore is nearly everywhere and the tin bottleneck that had
made bronze a strategic problem simply dissolved. But iron did not rebuild the trading world. That
was done by a handful of small coastal cities on the Levantine shore -- Byblos, Sidon, Arwad and
above all Tyre -- whose Canaanite inhabitants the Greeks called *Phoinikes*, and by the Cypriots
alongside them.

Why those two and not others? The answer that has emerged is not luck.

The Canaanites of the Levantine coast were not newcomers; they were the survivors of the
Bronze Age cities, carrying on in the same places under a new name. What they were not was imperial.
Carol Bell's formulation is the sharpest: Cyprus and Phoenicia "were able to seize the day when
crisis struck the region", being "unencumbered by imperial agendas, and already familiar with
operating within a decentralised trading environment", so that their traders "remained open for
business, with their primary objective being to generate sufficient returns to continue to trade".
Eric Cline goes further and calls both societies anti-fragile: they did not merely survive the
collapse but flourished in the chaos that followed it, the Phoenicians taking the sack of Ugarit and
the other port cities as their opportunity to win control of the Mediterranean routes, the Cypriots
doing the same with iron goods and iron technology. The economies that failed in 1177 were
centralised, redistributive and tightly coupled. What replaced them at the centre of Mediterranean
exchange was a set of merchant cities with no empire and no great king -- which is the chapter's
lesson about coupling, restated from the other side.^[**Sources:** Cline, *After 1177 B.C.: The
Survival of Civilizations* (2021), ch. 3, "The Mediterranean Became a Phoenician Lake", for the
continuity of the Canaanite population, the anti-fragile reading of Phoenicia and Cyprus, and the
Carol Bell quotation; Pilkington, *The Carthaginian Empire, 550-202 BCE*, on the Levantine cities
after the collapse. Cited by chapter: the held edition is an EPUB without pagination.
**Read more:** Cline (2021).]

One document shows the change better than any argument about it. Around 1075 BCE an Egyptian temple
official named Wenamun was sent from Karnak to Byblos to buy cedar for a ceremonial barge. In the
Amarna world of two centuries earlier this would have been a matter between courts. It was not any
more. Wenamun was robbed at Dor on the way; the prince of Byblos, Tjekkerbaal, received him with open
hostility; and the timber was not cut until payment had been shipped from Egypt and inspected. The
payment is itemised, and reads like an invoice: four gold bowls and another gold vessel, five bowls
of silver, ten pieces of clothing, five hundred mats of smooth linen, five hundred ox hides, five
hundred ropes, twenty sacks of lentils and five baskets of fish. Only then did the prince detail
three hundred men and three hundred oxen to fell the trees, which lay through the winter before
being hauled to the shore. An Egyptian priest could no longer requisition Lebanese cedar on the
strength of who he served. He had to buy it, in advance, from a man who was free to be rude to him.
That is the shift from the gift economy the Uluburun ship was carrying to a price economy, recorded
in one bad-tempered voyage.^[**Sources:** Cline, *After 1177 B.C.* (2021), ch. 3, quoting and
discussing the Tale of Wenamun, with the itemised payment and the felling of the timber; the
voyage is dated to about 1075 BCE. The Tale is a literary text of uncertain historicity, and should
be taught as a story that reflects commercial conditions rather than as a transaction record.
**Read more:** Cline (2021), ch. 3.]

The most famous thing they made was a colour, and it is the cleanest illustration the ancient world
offers of a price set by scarce supply meeting status-driven demand rather than by the cost of the
raw material.

Purple dye comes from a gland that has
to be cut from a living sea snail, with the shell broken to reach it, which is why the archaeological
signature of a dye-works is a bed of crushed shells rather than whole ones. The quantities are
brutal.

Experimental archaeology puts about two hundred snails into a square of wool 125 centimetres
on a side to reach a deep purple, and at least five thousand into a whole cloak; older estimates ran
to twenty thousand animals for a garment's trim alone. A batch took four days at minimum, and the
work stank badly enough that Strabo, centuries later, thought it made Tyre unpleasant to live in.
It would be wrong to conclude that the labour made the value — if effort made things valuable, every laborious process would be lucrative.

What made purple dear was that an inelastic, labour-bound supply met courts that would pay almost anything for a colour only they were permitted to wear.

States knew exactly where that left them. In a Hittite letter of the early thirteenth century a vassal
complains that a raid has cost him his purple-dyers -- three groups of them, one his own, one the
king's, one belonging to a god -- and the diplomatic effort to recover them is the substance of the
letter. Skilled dyers were capital, and were treated as such.^[**Sources:** Silver, *The Purpled
World* (2023), reporting Ruscillo's experimental work on murex yields and the Hittite correspondence
on captured dyers. Note that the held copy of Silver lacks book pagination, so these are cited by
section; the underlying experimental figures are Ruscillo (2005). **Read more:** Silver (2023).]

From the tenth century these cities founded settlements westward --- Cyprus first, then North Africa,
Sardinia and Sicily, and by about 800 to 780 BCE, on radiocarbon dates, southern Spain. Among them
was *Qart Hadasht*, New City, which is Carthage. The traditional date for Carthage's foundation, 814 BCE, is a Greek
chronographer's arithmetic rather than an excavated one; the archaeology says late ninth or early
eighth century and declines to say more. Carthage was nobody yet. Through
this chapter's period it was a modest, peripheral, largely mud-brick town, one of the least
archaeologically visible of the western foundations, and the empire it later built belongs to the
next chapter, not this one.^[**Sources:** Pilkington, *The Carthaginian Empire*, on the western
foundation sequence, the radiocarbon dating of the Iberian settlements, the status of the 814 BCE
tradition, and Carthage's archaeological invisibility before about 650 BCE. **Read more:** Pilkington.]

What drove them west is the interesting question, and it is genuinely open. The traditional answer
is metals. Silver was becoming a proto-currency across the Iron Age Near East -- thirty-four silver
hoards have been recovered from Cisjordan alone -- and demand for it was sharpened by three things
at once: the collapse of the Bronze Age exchange networks, the Levant's own lack of silver, and the
rise of the Neo-Assyrian empire with its appetite for tribute. On this reading, first argued at
length by Susan Frankenstein and developed by Maria Eugenia Aubet, the western settlements were
commercial factories and the whole diaspora was a response to Assyrian pressure on Tyre. The
mining frontiers do open when the model predicts, in south-western Spain and at Laurion in the
Aegean.

The case against is archaeological, and it is not that the metals trade did not happen but
that it does not explain the settlements: the excavated colonies look like farms, agricultural towns
from their foundation. The argument is set out in @sec-appE. This chapter takes the position the
evidence supports and no more: the metals demand was real, the settlements were more than trading
posts, and the westward silver flow that the tidiest version of the story wants remains an inference
rather than a demonstrated fact.^[**Sources:** López-Ruiz and
Doak (eds), *The Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean* (2019), for the Iron Age
silver economy and the Cisjordan hoards, for the Frankenstein thesis and Aubet's commercial-diaspora
development of it, and for the shift away from exclusively commercial explanations of colonization;
Pilkington, *The Carthaginian Empire*, p. 61, for the negative case and for the Huelva sherd counts,
sailing distances and agricultural character of the settlements. **Read more:** López-Ruiz and Doak
(2019).]

A word about the people already there, because this section has so far been told from the ships. The
society the Phoenicians met in south-western Iberia is known as Tartessos, and the temptation is to
file it as the native partner in a colonial encounter. Sebastián Celestino and Carolina López-Ruiz
argue that this gets the thing backwards. Tartessos, on their account, cannot be understood as an
impermeable entity separate from the contact: it *is* the cultural horizon that the contact
produced, formed from an indigenous substratum meeting several waves of Phoenician settlement, with
contributions from elsewhere in the Mediterranean at different stages. There was no fixed
Tartessian culture that the Phoenicians then traded with; the two made a third thing together.

It is also, they note, a society we know almost entirely through other people's writing, having left
no historical narrative of its own — which is the same evidential predicament as the Phoenicians
themselves, and a reason to be careful about who gets described as the active party in this
encounter.^[**Sources:** Celestino Pérez and López-Ruiz, *Tartessos and the Phoenicians in Iberia*
(Oxford University Press), for the argument that Tartessos is the product of contact rather than a
pre-existing entity encountered by it, and for the absence of self-generated written narratives.
**Read more:** Celestino Pérez and López-Ruiz.]

Two other things travelled with the pots. One was a script. Short Phoenician inscriptions, mostly
personal names and ownership marks, turn up scratched on ordinary locally made jars in the harbour
houses of Castillo de Dona Blanca near Gadir -- thirty-eight of them from the eighth and seventh
centuries -- and by the seventh century the Iberians around Gadir were writing too, on objects of
trade. This is writing as a merchant's tool rather than a bureaucracy's, and it is the counter-case to
Uruk. Cuneiform was expensive. It took hundreds of signs, a scribal career to learn them, and it
grew out of running a large institution's accounts. The Phoenician script was a consonantal
alphabet of twenty-two letters, one for each consonantal phoneme in the language, and a trader
could carry it in his head.

Its history matters because of when it spread. A consonantal alphabet had been adapted to the
cuneiform technique at Ugarit in the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BCE, but the schematised, reduced form
that became the Phoenician script came into common use around the twelfth century or a little
later -- in the specialists' own phrasing, with the reopening of trade links after the collapse.
From there it went everywhere: to the Israelites, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites and Aramaeans,
whose national scripts are all essentially its children; westward with the settlements; and into
the Aegean, where the Greeks adapted it, adding vowels. The oldest Greek alphabetic inscriptions
date to about the second quarter of the eighth century BCE, and the transmission is dated by
comparing letter shapes, since the Phoenician forms of the ninth and eighth centuries are the ones
the archaic Greek letters most resemble.

The economic point is the one to carry forward. When the cost of learning to record a transaction
falls from a career to an afternoon, record-keeping stops being a function of the state. Uruk's
accounting produced a scribal class; Tyre's produced a merchant class that could write. Both are
answers to the same problem, and the second is very much cheaper.^[**Sources:** López-Ruiz and Doak
(eds), *The Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean* (2019), on the twenty-two-
letter consonantal alphabet and its match to Phoenician phonology, the Ugaritic cuneiform
antecedent, the schematised script emerging around the twelfth century with the reopening of trade
links, its spread through the Levantine national scripts, and the dating of the Greek adaptation by
grapheme comparison, with the oldest Greek inscriptions in the second quarter of the eighth century.
The claim that the script's cheapness had economic consequences is this book's inference from those
facts, not a finding the handbook states. **Read more:** López-Ruiz and Doak (2019).]

The other thing that travelled was competition. Within two centuries the neighbours had learned the
writing, the farming and the politics, and Greek settlement in the western Mediterranean came to
outnumber Phoenician. Settler counts measure presence rather than commercial advantage, so read that
as a sign and not a measurement --- but what it points at, advantage decaying by imitation once the
technique is cheap to copy, is a pattern this book will meet again in Venice, in Amsterdam and in
Lancashire.^[**Sources:** Pilkington, *The
Carthaginian Empire*, on the Castillo de Dona Blanca inscriptions, indigenous Iberian writing at
Gadir, and the relative numbers of Greek and Phoenician settlers by 600 BCE. **Note on a gap:** the
held corpus supports the archaeology of merchant literacy but not the history of the alphabet
itself -- its letter count, its date, or the mechanism of its transmission to Greek. Those claims are
deliberately not made here. **Read more:** Pilkington.]

By 500 BCE the pieces of the next order were in place. Persia had reunited the Near East, iron had
loosened the tin bottleneck, the Lydians had struck the first coins and the Greeks were already
minting small change. Carthage, still a modest city, had founded its own first colony, Ebusus, back in 654 BCE.
The board was reset, and the story hands on to the next chapter, where the channels would fuse into
the first genuinely trans-Eurasian system.

## Reading the period: the four questions

The three thousand years from about 3500 to 500 BCE can be put through the same four questions that drive the rest of this book, with the warning that the answers here are softer than any later chapter's, because the evidence is thinner and the system looser. They are worth running all the same, because this is where the questions themselves are forged.

The first question was about direction: was the system integrating or disintegrating? The answer was that it did both, repeatedly, and that no single arc ran through the period. An early integrated sphere, the so-called Uruk world system, reached from the Iranian plateau to the eastern Mediterranean around 3500 BCE and then contracted near 3000 BCE as its long-distance networks thinned. The Gulf trade that linked the Indus to Mesopotamia rose after that and unwound in its turn. The eastern-Mediterranean palace economies knit themselves tightly together across the second millennium and then came apart around 1177 BCE in the Late Bronze Age Collapse, when mainland Greece may have lost something between forty and sixty per cent of its people. The pattern was a sequence of integration-then-fragmentation cycles, the module's rhythm in miniature, and the lesson it bequeathed to every later chapter was that integration bred fragility: the routes that carried trade also carried shocks, and a more connected system was a more exposed one.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 1199); Kriwaczek (Page 72); Cline (Loc 507). **Read more:** Cline, *1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed* (2014).]

The second question was about channels, and this period's answer is that all three of the module's corridors were born here at once. The maritime Indian Ocean, the desert and oasis route that would later be called the Silk Road, and the great Eurasian steppe all took shape in these millennia.

Of the three, the steppe was the era's dynamic engine, not its periphery: a band of unbroken grass running some seven thousand kilometres from eastern Europe to the Great Wall of China, across which mounted herders moved at a pace no one on foot could match. The ocean, the corridor this book centres on, was still largely waiting, its monsoon geography laid down but its traffic thin.

To see how the channels actually worked, it helps to follow one good through the system, and the most revealing is tin. Bronze, the period's defining metal, needed tin, yet tin lay almost nowhere near the cities that used it, so it had to travel long distances to reach them.

Its price marked the route. Quoted in silver, 100 shekels of tin cost about 6.7 shekels of silver at Assur, about 10 at Mari and about 14.3 in Anatolia. Tin was worth roughly twice as much at the western end, and that gap pulled the metal across.

This was price-responsive long-distance trade operating centuries before any coin existed to express it, visible only in the barter ratios that the cuneiform records preserve. The volumes were not trivial either: a single cargo such as the one lost off Uluburun around 1300 BCE carried perhaps a tonne of tin in one hull.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe (Loc 158, 909); Frahm (Page 47); Anthony (Loc 6829); Cline (Loc 1646). **Read more:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015).]

::: {.callout-important}
## Follow the money
With no coins yet, the period's bullion tracer was the relative price of metals, and tin is the clearest one to track. It had to travel because bronze needed it and it lay far from the cities that consumed it. The gap between its price at Assur, about 6.7 shekels of silver per 100 shekels of tin, and in Anatolia, about 14.3, moved the metal from where it was cheap toward where it was dear, centuries before coinage. The gap is also a measurement: roughly a doubling over 950 kilometres is what carriage cost in this technology, and later chapters watch that wedge narrow. This is the same "follow the metal" logic the module will use for millennia to locate the centre, except that here it shows up in barter ratios scratched onto clay rather than in the output of any mint.
:::

![The price of distance: 100 shekels of tin cost about 6.7 shekels of silver at Assur but about 14.3 in Anatolia, where it was scarcer. The gap is not arbitrage --- it is the cost of carriage, quoted, centuries before any coin existed to express it, and integration is that wedge narrowing (stylised; values from the Old Assyrian records). Source: Frahm.](book/figures/tin-arbitrage-01.png){#fig-tin width=72%}

It was not only raw metal that moved. High-value processed goods travelled too, and they mattered out of proportion to their bulk, because a supply that could not easily be expanded met a demand that would pay almost anything.

Ugarit, for one, paid its yearly tribute to the Hittites not only in gold but in dyed wool and finished garments, cloth being among the most concentrated stores of value a Bronze Age economy could ship. The vivid later case of such a luxury is Tyrian purple, the dye won at enormous labour from murex sea-snails, whose extreme cost made it a marker of rank for the rest of antiquity. Here a caution is needed. One scholar, Morris Silver, has read the Aegean Bronze Age textile and purple trade as evidence of a far more commercialised, market-like world than the orthodox picture allows, even casting the Trojan War as a trade war; that bolder reading is a contested hypothesis rather than settled fact, and is best treated as one provocative interpretation of the same material that more cautious accounts read as palace-administered exchange.^[**Sources:** Cline (Loc 2308); on the market-formalist reading of Aegean Bronze Age purple and textiles as a contested hypothesis, Silver, *The Purpled World* (2023). **Read more:** Cline, *1177 B.C.* (2014).]

![*Bolinus brandaris*, the murex sea-snail from which Tyrian purple was won at enormous labour --- the vivid later case of a processed luxury whose value lay in the work locked into it. Photo: H. Zell, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.](book/figures/photos/murex.jpg){#fig-murex width=52%}

![A single Bronze Age cargo as a dataset of one: the Uluburun wreck (c.1300 BCE) carried ~10 tonnes of copper and ~1 tonne of tin --- the ~10:1 bronze recipe --- plus glass, resin, ivory and amber, with products of at least nine or ten cultures. Bulk metal moved by sea long before coins (estimated tonnages). Source: Cline.](book/figures/uluburun-cargo-01.png){#fig-uluburun width=66%}

The third question was about modes: what crossed the connection? Two kinds of thing did, and the chapter is clearer if they are kept apart.

On one side are real flows, and the production function names them. Output itself moves as goods. Useful knowledge moves as technique. People move as labour. Produced assets move as capital. On the other side run monetary and financial flows: things that settle a transaction, and claims that carry purchasing power across time. Silver sits on both sides at once, which is the complication this period is best at teaching.

Take them in turn, because the evidence for each is a different instrument.

**Goods (Y) are somebody else's land, arriving in usable form.** A cargo of tin is a mineral endowment that Mesopotamia did not have. That is what makes tin and not grain the story: a small flow of an input nothing can substitute for has more structural consequence than a large flow of something anybody can grow.

There is also one piece of evidence here for the other side of the equation, and the archaeology of trade almost never reaches it. Demand. Ancient proteins recovered from dental calculus at Bronze Age Megiddo, around 1650 to 1320 BCE, record what individual people actually put in their mouths: cereals, sesame and dates as expected, and then soybean in one individual, turmeric in one, probable banana in one. At least one person in the second-millennium Levant ate a South Asian spice and a South Asian pulse.

Be exact about what that licenses. It establishes contact. It is silent on commerce. It cannot say how many, how often, or whether a market existed, and every exotic in the study rests on a single person. The study's authors read it less cautiously than this and write of a pattern of established trade; the gap between what evidence licenses and what is claimed from it, including by the people who produced it, is worth more to an economist than the finding.^[**Sources:** Scott et al. (2021) on the Megiddo and Tel Erani dental calculus; the identifications rest on two and three peptides respectively, at or barely above the standard authentication threshold. **Note:** there is no published rebuttal of these identifications --- the caution here is this book's reading of a general methodological standard, not a critique in the literature. **Read more:** Scott et al., "Exotic foods reveal contact between South Asia and the Near East", *PNAS* 118 (2021).]

**Technology (A) moved, and it moved slowly.** The chariot took something like eight hundred years to cross a continent, from Sintashta graves east of the Urals before 2000 BCE to China around 1200. That is the diffusion speed of this world, and it is the baseline against which every later chapter's should be read.

**People (L) moved, and two studies measure it in a way no document can.** The Harappan cemeteries are the first. Strontium and lead isotopes in tooth enamel, seventy-seven teeth from fifty-five individuals at Harappa and Farmana, and the design is what makes the result strong: the three molars form at different ages, so one skeleton yields an ordered sequence of childhood residences rather than an average. First molars fall outside the local range. Second and third converge on it, at Farmana around three to five years of age. These were not locals. They were first-generation immigrants.

The economics is in where they came from. The migrants point north-west to the upper Indus and north-east to the Punjab plains, and the lead in the Farmana burials points at the Khetri copper belt about a hundred and fifty kilometres south. Migrants and metals travelled the same corridors. Resource peripheries exported the material and the people who knew how to get it, and that is a relationship this chapter meets again at its far end, in Cornwall.

The sample will not carry a migration rate, and the reason is a selection rule rather than a small sample size. Fewer than six hundred Indus skeletons exist from a century of excavation across some 680,000 square kilometres, and formal cemetery burial is rare within that. A cemetery here is not a thin random sample of Indus society. It is a complete sample of a small institution.^[**Sources:** Valentine et al. (2015) on strontium and lead isotopes at Harappa and Farmana. **Caveats the authors state:** the local range is defined from faunal samples whose spread suggests some of the animals were themselves imported, which makes the non-local verdict conservative but is an inference; breastfeeding by immigrant mothers and childhood exposure to imported lead-bearing cosmetics are argued against rather than eliminated; the South Asian ore and slag reference data are in the authors' own word equivocal. **Read more:** Valentine et al., *PLOS ONE* 10 (2015).]

The second study is in Britain, and it measures a flow of people with no price attached to it at all. Five isotope systems run on 131 pigs from four Late Neolithic henge complexes in southern Britain, around 2800 to 2400 BCE. The strontium range at Durrington Walls is wider than at any other published British site, wider than a Roman legionary fortress sitting on far more varied geology. Three kilometres away, Middle Neolithic animals from West Amesbury Farm show the narrowest range of any British assemblage.

So the wide catchment is not a property of the landscape. It is new, and it is institutional.

The economics turns on the animal. Pigs drive badly over distance, and there is no reason to walk one for hundreds of kilometres rather than carry the meat, unless the animal and the people who raised it are meant to arrive together. The isotopes are therefore measuring the geographic reach of a mobilisation organised without money, writing, prices or a market. Hold it in mind for Q4: peripheral in a network is not the same thing as simple.^[**Sources:** Madgwick et al. (2019), the largest fully published multi-isotope faunal dataset in archaeology. **Caveat:** provenance here is by exclusion --- the animals are shown not to be local, not traced to farms --- and with thin British comparative data for sulfur and oxygen, most of the geographic weight rests on strontium. **Read more:** Madgwick et al., *Science Advances* 5 (2019).]

**Capital (K) was present and thin.** Ships, pack animals, irrigation works, workshops and stores are the capital of this world, and there is nothing in it that could be called a capital market.

That last point needs care, because finance in this period was sophisticated without being broad, and the two are easy to confuse. Money and credit are not capital. They are what let capital be assembled and what bridges the delay between committing resources and getting them back.

That delay is the thing to picture. Assur to Kanesh was about 950 kilometres and roughly fifty days each way, with perhaps a hundred days between committing goods and seeing any silver return. Fifty-odd donkeys, fodder, drivers and tolls all had to be paid for in advance. A trade with that shape cannot run on cash in hand.

So it ran on credit, and we know it did because the Kanesh archive is a merchant archive: some twelve thousand private letters and account tablets from the trading families themselves rather than from a palace. For once in this period we are reading the traders. The claims and obligations in those letters are denominated in silver, across households and across a political frontier, with no coin anywhere in the system.

The institutional depth goes back further. Interest-bearing debt is securely attested from the later third millennium and may reach to about 3000 BCE; Hammurabi's ceilings of twenty per cent on silver and thirty-three and a third on barley codified a practice that was already old. And rulers periodically wiped the slate. The earliest recorded is Enmetena of Lagash, around 2400 BCE, and the Sumerian word for what he granted was *amargi*, literally a return to the mother, debtors going home. It is the earliest attested word for freedom in any written language.

The first freedom in the written record is freedom from debt.

One last flow belongs here, and it complicates this book's own spine before the spine has started. Before coinage, silver in the Levant circulated as hacksilver, cut and weighed, and because it was not endlessly remelted its lead-isotope signature reads onto the ore field that was worked. Seventy-five items from three dated Phoenician hoards show the source moving: Anatolian silver is prominent in the tenth and ninth centuries, but by the ninth-century hoard at Ein Hofez only two of twenty-nine items are consistent with Anatolian ore and most point to Iberia.

The metal is running west to east. Students arrive expecting silver always to flow toward Asia, because that is what @sec-ch05 and @sec-ch06 will show them. The first traceable flow in the record does the opposite. Direction is a function of where the ore sits and where the demand sits, and both of those move.^[**Sources:** Eshel et al. (2019) on lead isotopes in hacksilver from Dor, Akko and Ein Hofez; Frahm (Page 47) and Goetzmann (loc 592, 836) on Old Assyrian credit; Graeber (Loc 8075, 4560) on the *amargi* cancellations; Barjamovic, Chaney, Cosar and Hortacsu (2019), *QJE* 134(3), on the Kanesh corpus. **Caveats:** many hacksilver items are mixtures rather than single-source, and copper-alloyed hoards were excluded from the study, which is a selection rule of unknown direction. Graeber's wider debt-before-barter thesis is contested; the specific Mesopotamian facts here are not, and Goetzmann is the safer citation for the finance-history framing. **Read more:** Goetzmann, *Money Changes Everything* (2016).]

The fourth question was about Europe, and this is the answer that has changed most.

The old line was that Bronze Age Europe sat outside the world system whose cores were in West Asia and the Indian Ocean. That is not right, and the thing that changed it is tin.

Start with why the question was stuck for so long. The obstacle was never the artefacts. It was that nobody had characterised the ores, so there was nothing to compare an ingot against. A Durham-led programme built the reference base: 142 ores analysed for trace elements, 98 for lead isotopes, 23 for tin isotopes, against more than two hundred tin artefacts. Baselines before comparisons.

Then a two-step discrimination. Cornish and Devon cassiterites carry up to 176 parts per million of indium where Iberian and French ores are under ten, and indium survives smelting, which is what makes it readable on an ingot rather than on a rock. That removes Iberia and France. Lead-isotope model age separates the two survivors: the Erzgebirge comes out at 318 to 323 million years, Cornwall and Devon at 274 to 293. Tin from three radiocarbon-dated Israeli wrecks gives 290. Rochelongue, off southern France and much later, gives 278. Both sit inside Cornwall and well outside the Erzgebirge.

One sentence keeps that honest in a seminar: tin isotopes alone cannot do this job, because the tin provinces overlap too much. The work is done by indium and by lead-isotope model age. A summary crediting "tin isotope analysis" with settling the question has misread the paper, and a good many of them do.

What is settled is the Cornish case for the Israeli wrecks and for Rochelongue. What is not settled is Uluburun, where two laboratories read the same cargo and reach incompatible answers: one programme puts the ingots inside Cornish and Devon ranges, another attributes roughly two-thirds to the Taurus and a third to Central Asia, three thousand kilometres east. Concede the strongest point against the Cornish reading rather than smoothing it --- the Uluburun ingots measure 2 to 7 parts per million of indium against up to 176 in Cornish ore, and indium is the discriminator. The verdict here rests on the Israeli wrecks, not on Uluburun.^[**Sources:** Williams et al. (2025) for the Durham ore programme, the indium discrimination and the model ages; Powell et al. (2022) for the Taurus and Musiston attribution of 105 Uluburun ingots; Berger et al. (2023) for the indium measurements that cut against the Cornish reading of that cargo. **Worth knowing:** Berger is a co-author on two of the three, so the lines of evidence are less independent than they look, and lead-isotope provenancing at Uluburun is compromised by lead contamination running from 22 ppm to 11.5 per cent. **Read more:** Williams et al. (2025).]

So the answer to Q4 is not "peripheral" in the sense students expect. Britain supplied tin, without which there is no bronze, to a network whose demand, capital, weights, writing and organisation all sat in West Asia. That is a resource periphery *inside* the system, which is a different thing from being outside it.

Make the production model concrete, because it is what makes "periphery" precise rather than dismissive. The tin came from decentralised small alluvial workings, worked part-time alongside farming, handed to coastal trading places and passed down the line. There was no direct contact of any kind between Britain and the Levant. Nobody in Cornwall knew where the metal ended up and nobody in Ugarit knew where it started. Britain supplied an input. It did not organise, price or capture the trade in it.

Which is this chapter's sharpest instance of N as power, and the sentence is worth memorising because it recurs at Potosi, at Banda and at every commodity exporter in the twentieth century: **the holder of the scarce resource was not the holder of the rents.**

Now the scale, and be scrupulous with it. Perhaps 100 to 200 tonnes of tin a year across all of Europe and the Mediterranean in the mid-second millennium BCE --- and say the caveat in the same breath, because the authors call the figure speculative. It is scaled from copper output at three mines on an assumed ten per cent tin-to-copper ratio, then extrapolated across more than a hundred known mines. A number built by multiplying an uncertain quantity by an assumed coefficient inherits the uncertainty of both. For proportion: Cornwall and Devon produced about 400 tonnes a year in 1200 CE on substantially the same technology with some six thousand mainly part-time workers.

A strategic flow, then, and not a large one. Both halves are true.

None of which makes Europe simple. Varna on the Black Sea, around 4500 BCE, yielded some three thousand gold objects weighing roughly six kilograms, more gold than every other fifth-millennium find in the world put together. And the Durrington pigs show southern Britain mobilising animals from most of an island to one place. Organisational sophistication and peripheral position are independent facts, and this period has both.^[**Sources:** on scale and the production model, Williams et al. (2025); Anthony (Loc 3941) on Varna; Madgwick et al. (2019) on the Durrington catchment. **Read more:** Anthony, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* (2007).]

Behind all four questions stood the forces this module tracks. Geography came first: the Himalayan uplift, the monsoon and the great rivers set the board. Climate was the first dynamic driver, its swings bearing on the rise and fall of cores. And technology --- the sail married to monsoon knowledge, the horse, the wheel, bronze --- turned geographic possibility into movement.

## Which input was binding?

Every chapter in this book closes its analysis with the same line of the ledger: which input was doing the work, and which one was in the way?

**N was binding, everywhere, and it bound in two different ways.** As a level: there was no tin in Mesopotamia, and Uruk hauled its stone eighty kilometres, so a bronze-using city had to be connected to a continent whether it wanted to be or not. As variance: the river under the Indus cities was not short of water so much as unreliable about it. Two kinds of scarcity, one input, and the second is the one students miss.

**A moved, and moved slowest.** Eight hundred years for the chariot to cross a continent.

**L was the residual claimant.** A better technique or a windfall of land was captured as more people rather than as higher income per head. That is Malthus written in this book's notation, and it is why the period's thriving is counted in cities and populations.

**K was real but thin, and finance was sophisticated without being broad.** Credit crossed a political frontier at Assur and Kanesh centuries before anyone struck a coin. It was also relationship-based, running between known households and named agents, and there is nothing in this world that resembles an impersonal capital market.

And control of N is where the economic power sat: Dilmun taking a cut at a chokepoint without producing anything, Cyprus with its copper, Cornwall with its tin. The finding to carry forward is the one Q4 just delivered. Britain had the tin. West Asia had the trade.

## The verdict: where was the centre?

The verdict for this period is that there was no single centre, and it is delivered with low confidence by design.

What the evidence shows is several loosely linked riverine cores rather than one integrated world economy with a weight that can be located. The Near East, and Uruk above all, was the most central node, a large urban demand pole and the supplier of metals into the long-distance trade. The Indus led the Gulf trade through its mature phase, and it survives as a bright spot in a thin record rather than as a documented centre.

Be exact about which way that thinness cuts. Because the humid tropics destroy organic evidence, what survives from the Indus is a lower bound on its activity rather than an estimate of it. That licenses a claim about direction — there was more there than we can see — and it licenses nothing about magnitude. What it does not license is treating the sparseness of the record as though it were evidence for the argument, which is a move this chapter made in an earlier draft and should not make. Egypt and the forming East Asian core sat largely apart from the western-Eurasian system that the evidence actually documents.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 805); Frahm (Page 46). **Read more:** Frahm, *Assyria* (2023).]

This is where the chapter must say plainly what it cannot do. The centre-of-gravity question that runs through the rest of the book — whether the weight of the world economy sat in Asia, and whether it was moving — is not yet applicable here. This period neither supports nor contradicts the claim that Asia was central, because it predates a connected system in which a centre of gravity is even a meaningful idea. There were cores, but they were not yet bound tightly enough into one economy for the question to be asked, let alone tested. The first chapter at which the question becomes answerable is the next one, when Alexander and the Achaemenid inheritance fuse the channels into something like a single trans-Eurasian system. What this chapter contributes is therefore structural rather than evidential. It lays down the monsoon and the channel geography that will later make the Indian Ocean the natural integrator and centre the very system the book goes on to track.^[**Sources:** Pearson (Ch.1) on the monsoon deep structure and the channels. **Read more:** Pearson, *The Indian Ocean* (2003).]

The denominator has to be kept honest. These were overwhelmingly agrarian subsistence economies in which the great majority farmed and never handled a trade good; the long-distance traffic described here was a thin and lucrative network laid over that mass, not the bulk of output. And a second caution governs what "success" can mean in this world. Whatever thriving the period shows was measured in numbers, not income per head: more food meant more people rather than richer people, the Malthusian condition humanity shared with every other species. The switch from measuring an economy by its scale to measuring it by the living standards of the people in it lies far ahead, at the Great Divergence of @sec-ch07. Hold the two apart from the start: aggregate weight now, per-capita prosperity much later.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 631). **Read more:** Scott, *Against the Grain* (2017).]

::: {.callout-warning}
## The debate: how much weight should geography carry?
Cunliffe, and Diamond before him, lean hard on geography as the deciding force — the mountains and monsoon and grass corridors setting what was possible. The counter stresses human agency and contingency, the choices that geography permitted but did not dictate. The climate-collapse story is contested in the same way. The 4.2 ka weakening of the monsoon is invoked behind the Harappan decline, and drought behind the Late Bronze Age Collapse, yet the palaeo-record does not cleanly show a sharp, sustained drought at the right moment, so mono-causal climate accounts overreach. The sensible posture is to hold both at once: deep structures shaped the board on which the period was played, but people still chose the moves. Name the positions, weigh them, and leave the question genuinely open.
:::

**Data exhibit — the Uluburun cargo, a dataset of one.** With almost no quantitative records, a single well-excavated shipwreck does the work that a price series does in later chapters. The cargo is itemised above, and @fig-uluburun plots the two metals. *What you could do with this:* infer how many separate economies one hull implicates, and ask what the copper-to-tin ratio implies about where the metals were sourced and where the bronze was to be made — reasoning from one rich object to a whole system, with the uncertainty stated.

## Threads forward

What this chapter hands on is not a verdict but a period fully described: a world of loosely linked riverine cores, three cycles of integration and collapse, and the first evidence that connection carries shocks as well as goods. That last lesson — integration breeds fragility — runs from the Late Bronze Age Collapse through every later disintegration the book meets.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 631); Cline (Loc 507). **Read more:** Findlay & O'Rourke, *Power and Plenty* (2007).]

The hand-off to the next chapter is geographic and institutional at once. By about 500 BCE the Achaemenid empire had reunited the Near East, iron had loosened the tin bottleneck, and coinage had begun to standardise money. Alexander is where it turns, and the three channels born here would fuse into the first genuinely trans-Eurasian world system — Rome, Parthia, the Kushans and Han China strung along the routes — and the monsoon road this chapter laid down would become its maritime spine, with India at the fulcrum. At that point, for the first time, "where did the weight sit?" becomes a question the evidence can actually answer.^[**Sources:** on the Achaemenid reunification, iron and early coinage resetting the board. **Citation withdrawn:** this was attributed to Cline, *1177 B.C.*, but that book does not discuss the Achaemenid reunification and the word "coinage" does not appear in it; the claim needs a source that carries it. Schaps, *The Invention of Coinage and the Monetization of Ancient Greece* (2004), covers the coinage half. **Read more:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015).]

![The Alexander Mosaic (Pompeii) --- the turn into the next chapter, where Alexander and the Achaemenid inheritance fuse the three channels into the first trans-Eurasian world system. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.](book/figures/photos/div-alexander.jpg){#fig-alexander width=88%}

## Classic research: the foundations {.unnumbered}

The questions this chapter raises — was Bronze Age trade a market or a redistribution; how much weight should geography carry — descend from a bench of historians, archaeologists and anthropologists.

- **Polanyi (ed., 1957)**, *Trade and Market in the Early Empires* — the substantivist thesis that early "trade" was administered and redistributive rather than market exchange. The reference point for this chapter's central debate; the recent cliometric work below is the market-side rebuttal. Pair them.
- **Algaze (1993; 2008)**, *The Uruk World System* and *Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization* — the "Uruk world system" and the early peak-and-contraction that predates the Gulf trade.
- **Adams (1981)**, *Heartland of Cities* — the classic survey-archaeology of Mesopotamian urbanisation and settlement.
- **Sherratt (1981)**, "Plough and Pastoralism: Aspects of the Secondary Products Revolution," in *Pattern of the Past* — the traction/wool/dairy thesis; teach as contested (discrete event vs gradual adoption).
- **Possehl (2002)**, *The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective* — the standard synthesis and the "transformation, not collapse" reading of the Harappan decline.
- **Anthony (2007)**, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* — horse domestication, the Sintashta chariot, and the Indo-European expansions; the steppe-as-engine story.
- **Cline (2014)**, *1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed* — the systemic-fragility reading of the Late Bronze Age Collapse; this chapter's first "integration creates fragility" case.
- **Graeber (2011)**, *Debt: The First 5,000 Years* — credit, debt and the *amargi* cancellations; the case that finance preceded coinage.

## At the research frontier: recent cliometric work {.unnumbered}

A striking amount of recent economics reaches back into deep prehistory — fitting trade models to cuneiform tablets, and testing the origins of states, farming and the Malthusian regime. Every entry verified.

- **Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu (2019)**, "Trade, Merchants, and the Lost Cities of the Bronze Age," *Quarterly Journal of Economics* 134(3): 1455–1503 — a structural gravity model fit to ~12,000 Old Assyrian merchant tablets from Kanesh that recovers trade costs and even triangulates the locations of lost cities. The chapter's proof that Bronze Age long-distance trade was a genuine, estimable market. [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjz009]
- **Mayshar, Moav & Pascali (2022)**, "The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability?" *Journal of Political Economy* 130(4): 1091–1144 — hierarchy and taxation arose from the *appropriability* of storable cereals, not from higher farm productivity; the institutional micro-foundation under the riverine cores. [DOI 10.1086/718372]
- **Matranga (2024)**, "The Ant and the Grasshopper: Seasonality and the Invention of Agriculture," *Quarterly Journal of Economics* 139(3): 1467–1504 — rising climatic seasonality pushed foragers into storage and sedentism, the precondition for farming and surplus; grounds the chapter's "geography and climate as master force" in recent data. [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjae012]
- **Ashraf & Galor (2011)**, "Dynamics and Stagnation in the Malthusian Epoch," *American Economic Review* 101(5): 2003–2041 — the canonical empirical statement that, before 1800, technology and land raised population density rather than income per head. The frontier anchor for this chapter's quantity-vs-quality yardstick, and the thread it hands to @sec-ch07. [DOI 10.1257/aer.101.5.2003]

::: {.callout-note}
## Research in focus — Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu (2019): a gravity model on cuneiform
- **Aim** — to show that Bronze Age long-distance trade obeyed the same economic regularities as modern trade, and to use them to locate cities now lost.
- **Question** — can a structural gravity model, fit to ancient merchant records, recover trade costs and even the geographic position of unknown trading posts?
- **Data & method** — roughly 12,000 clay tablets from the Old Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh (early second millennium BCE), recording shipments between named cities; a structural gravity model in which trade falls with distance is fit to the recorded flows, and the locations of lost cities are estimated as the coordinates that best rationalise the trade pattern.
- **Findings** — trade fell with distance just as the modern gravity equation predicts; the model recovers sensible trade costs and places several lost cities close to where independent historical guesses had put them, with a few testable new predictions.
- **Caveats** — the data are one merchant network in one region and period, heavily weighted to tin and textiles; the gravity structure is imposed, not proven, and the city-location estimates are probabilistic.

*Sources: Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu, "Trade, Merchants, and the Lost Cities of the Bronze Age," Quarterly Journal of Economics 134(3), 2019 [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjz009].*
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Research in focus — Ashraf & Galor (2011): the Malthusian regime, and why "success" meant numbers
- **Aim** — to test the central prediction of the Malthusian model for the pre-industrial world: that productivity gains raised population, not living standards.
- **Question** — across the long pre-1800 era, did better technology and land translate into higher income per head, or simply into more people?
- **Data & method** — assembled cross-country data on population density and income for the pre-industrial period and related them to measures of technological and land productivity, testing the Malthusian mechanism.
- **Findings** — places with better technology and more productive land supported denser populations but not higher income per head; prosperity was converted into numbers, exactly as Malthus predicted, until the regime broke around 1800.
- **Caveats** — deep-history income and population figures are reconstructions with wide error bands; the result characterises the regime on average, not every local episode.

*Sources: Ashraf & Galor, "Dynamics and Stagnation in the Malthusian Epoch," American Economic Review 101(5), 2011 [DOI 10.1257/aer.101.5.2003]. The quantity-vs-quality distinction it formalises is the yardstick paid off at @sec-ch07.*
:::

---

### Questions for consideration {.unnumbered}

*Essay / exam style — reward the four-questions toolkit and the live debate, not recall.*

1. *"Before prices, how can we know a 'world economy' existed?"* Answer with Bronze Age evidence — the diffusion of goods, shared standards, and the direction of the ships.
2. *"Integration creates fragility."* Assess this claim using the Late Bronze Age Collapse and the contraction of the Uruk world system.
3. The Harappans ran the Gulf trade, yet the Indus survives as "a bright spot in a thin record." Explain how that thinness can *support* rather than undermine the claim that the record under-documents the East.
4. How much explanatory weight should climate carry in the end of the Harappan urban phase? Distinguish abrupt-forcing, gradual-hydrological, and multi-causal accounts.
5. *"Was Bronze Age trade a market, or redistribution?"* Use Mesopotamia (Polanyi) and the Kanesh tablet evidence (Barjamovic et al.) to frame both sides.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Cross-cutting questions (collected at the end of the book)
The book closes with a bank of questions spanning several chapters. Those this chapter opens:
- **Quantity vs quality.** This chapter introduces the distinction between aggregate ("more people") and per-capita ("richer people") success. Trace it through @sec-ch03, @sec-ch04 and @sec-ch07: when is a big economy legitimately a *rich* one?
- **Measuring integration.** Compare measuring integration by the diffusion of goods (this chapter) with measuring it by price convergence (@sec-ch08): what does each method see that the other misses?
:::

*This is the data-poorest chapter; the transferable skill is reasoning from proxies and single rich objects with the uncertainty stated, not from continuous series.*

### Further reading {.unnumbered}

- **Core:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015); Pearson, *The Indian Ocean* (2003), ch. 1; Scott, *Against the Grain* (2017).
- **Supplementary:** Anthony, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* (2007); Cline, *1177 B.C.* (2014); Possehl, *The Indus Civilization* (2002); Graeber, *Debt* (2011); Frahm, *Assyria* (2023); Kriwaczek, *Babylon* (2010).
- **The debate:** Polanyi (1957) and Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu (2019) on market vs redistribution; on geography and climate as master forces, Mayshar, Moav & Pascali (2022), Matranga (2024) and Ashraf & Galor (2011); on the Harappan decline, the palaeoclimate work of Staubwasser, Giosan and Gupta and colleagues, with Possehl's caution.
